# Dispatching work through sonata

**Date:** 2026-08-11

Notes from using sonata to implement its own provider-selection feature — eleven
of thirteen plan tasks were written by `deepseek-v4-flash` through
`opencode-go`, with three review runs on other models. Everything below was
observed on real runs, not reasoned about in advance.

## A task file must be self-contained

The obvious way to dispatch a planned task is "read the plan at `docs/.../x.md`
and do section 12". This fails once the plan is large. The provider-selection
plan is 2140 lines; the agent spent its whole context reading it and stopped,
its log ending:

```
Read docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-11-provider-selection.md [offset=1497]
The plan file output was truncated. Let me read the Task 12 section.
```

Extract the section — 320 lines here — and paste it into the task file instead.
The task text reaches the model directly and costs no tool calls.

Name the files the agent may read, and the ones it must not. Task 12 touched
six files totalling 2120 lines, and needed only three of them before its first
edit. Saying "do not read README.md, src/tui.ts, src/cli.ts" was the difference
between failing and succeeding.

## Split a task by what it must hold in context, not by what it delivers

Task 12 was one coherent deliverable — the two-step `init` flow — and it failed
twice as a single run. Split into the flow rewrite and then the CLI flag plus
README, both passed first try. Coherence is the right criterion when writing a
plan for a human; context footprint is the right criterion when dispatching it.

## Exit 0 is not success

A run that exhausts its context exits 0, writes no report, and leaves the tree
clean. Nothing distinguishes it from a no-op except the log. Check:

```bash
cat .sonata/runs/<id>/exit          # 0 proves only that nothing crashed
wc -c .sonata/runs/<id>/harness.log # a few hundred bytes means it barely started
git log --oneline -1                # did the commit it claims exist?
```

A log containing only `Read` lines means the agent ran out of room.

## Verify the work, not the report

Agent reports are confident and sometimes wrong about their own effects. For
each task, check the commit's diff and file count, that the trailers are
present, and run the full suite yourself. Two things worth checking that no
unit test covers:

- Run the new parser over real data. `parseOpenCodeRefs` was verified against a
  live 496-line `opencode models` catalogue — 496 parsed, none lost, and
  `openrouter/~anthropic/claude-fable-latest` split correctly.
- Drive the state machine directly for invariants a green suite can hide. The
  filtering rewrite hinged on `checked` holding original indices while `cursor`
  indexes the filtered view; a script proving a checked item survives filtering
  is stronger evidence than the tests asserting it.

## Scope reviews to one file

A review of a fifteen-commit diff hit `run_timeout_seconds` (1800s, exit 143)
with no output. The same work split one file per run finished in minutes, and
found a real defect: `tomlFor` escaped its TOML table header but interpolated
`generate.models` raw, so a key containing a quote produced a config that no
longer parsed.

Give the reviewer the invariants to hunt and tell it to say plainly when a
category is clean. Otherwise a review of correct code produces plausible
suggestions rather than a finding of nothing.

## Parallel dispatch is bounded by the gateway, not by the work

Generic parallel-dispatch guidance — including
`superpowers:dispatching-parallel-agents` — decides concurrency from the
*tasks*: independent problem domains, no shared state, fan out. Through sonata
that is only half the question, because agents that share nothing in the
repository still share one upstream.

Measured 2026-09-16 while executing an eleven-task plan with seven agents on a
single `codex-oauth` gateway: **three agents died mid-run** on an upstream
`400 — No tool output found for function call`, and a fourth hit **529 with
every native candidate exhausted**. Task independence bought nothing there;
the tier's eleven candidates were all effort variants of two models behind one
subscription, so they queued behind each other, failed, and cooled down
together. The work survived only because each agent committed before it
crashed, and the one that did not had its work verified and committed by hand.

So pick concurrency from what the *gateway* can carry:

- Count the distinct upstreams, not the distinct tasks. Eleven ranked
  candidates on one subscription is one upstream.
- A tier that exhausts returns 529 naming `sonata dispatch --tier`, which is
  the harness lane — a real fallback, but it runs outside the router. (When
  this was written its tokens never reached the ledger; since 0.13.0 a
  finished dispatch is measured from the harness's own store, recorded in the
  ledger, and counted toward `[budget]`.)
- Expect crashes rather than preventing them: have every agent commit its own
  work, scoped to the files it owns, so a death costs one agent's turn rather
  than the wave.

### Never let an agent run `git stash` — worktrees do not save you

`refs/stash` is a single repository-wide ref, so the stash stack is shared by
every linked worktree. Verified 2026-09-17 on a scratch repo: agent 1 ran
`git stash` in worktree `wt1`; agent 2, in worktree `wt2` on a *different
branch*, saw that entry in `git stash list`, popped it, and ended up holding
agent 1's edits — which were gone from agent 1's tree and dropped from the
stack. Neither agent did anything wrong, and nothing errored.

So isolation by worktree is not a defence here. Put the prohibition in every
agent prompt, whichever layout you use, along with the other repository-global
or neighbour-destroying commands:

- `git stash` (any form) — shared stack, as above
- `git reset --hard`, `git checkout -- .`, `git clean -fd` — discard whatever
  uncommitted work other agents have in a shared tree
- `git add -A`, `git commit -a` — stage a neighbour's in-flight edits into your
  commit
- `git checkout <branch>` in a shared checkout — moves every agent's HEAD

The positive form is one line: **stage the paths you own, commit them, and
touch nothing else.**

### Shared checkout or one worktree per agent?

Default to a **shared checkout with exclusive file ownership**, and reach for
worktrees only when the tasks are genuinely disjoint.

The reason is that plans are less independent than they look. In the
eleven-task run above, task 1 widened a shared type and that was a compile
error in three files owned by tasks 5, 8 and a file no task owned — 7 errors
in total. In a shared tree the owning agents fixed them as they landed, and
every later agent verified against an integrated state. In separate worktrees
each of those agents would have been staring at errors it was forbidden to fix,
in files it could not see being repaired, and the integration would have
happened at merge time with nobody watching.

Worktrees earn their cost when tasks touch genuinely separate subsystems, share
no types, and each wants to run a long suite without seeing a neighbour's
half-applied change. The costs are real: `npm install` per worktree, N merges
instead of none, and — specific to this repository — `sonata.toml` is untracked,
so a worktree borrows the main checkout's config (`mainWorktreeDir`), while
`.claude/settings.local.json` cannot be borrowed at all and routing must be set
up in the worktree itself.

Two rules made a shared checkout safe for seven concurrent agents, and both are
worth keeping whatever the concurrency:

**Give every agent exclusive file ownership**, and say so in its prompt —
"modify only these paths; if the task seems to need another, stop and report
it". Seven agents produced no merge conflict under that rule.

**Never `git add -A`.** Each agent stages only its own paths. This is written
here because the one place it was violated in that session was the coordinator's
own commit, which swept up another agent's in-flight edits and a stray scratch
file, and split one task's history across two commits under a misleading
message.

**Substitute tier agents for `general-purpose`.** That skill's examples all
dispatch `general-purpose`, which runs on Claude and ends the foreign-model
lane silently — the subagent works, reports, and looks exactly like a routed
one. Dispatch `code-*`, `review-*`, `explore-*` or `plan-*` instead, and omit
the `model` argument: the tier is the model choice.

## Model notes

`grok-4.5` did not complete either review dispatched to it — one hit the 1800s
timeout, the other produced 29 bytes of output in forty minutes, both with a
blank pane. `kimi-k3` and `gpt-5.6-terra` completed the same shape of review in
minutes. `deepseek-v4-flash` handled every mechanical task in the plan and,
given a literal specification, reproduced it faithfully; it also caught a test
fixture the plan had not listed.

This is one afternoon's evidence on one machine, not a benchmark.

## A read-only role cannot write its report

Dogfooding surfaced a real defect. A review run ended:

> Unable to write the required report because plan mode prohibits file edits.

Read-only roles run under opencode's `plan` agent, which blocks writes, so
`report.md` can never be produced. The adapter did not say so, and `meta.json`
recorded `canWriteReport: true` — meaning every review and plan run on opencode
was judged degraded for a file it was structurally incapable of writing. Fixed
by keying `canWriteReport` off the agent actually chosen, since `explore` is
read-only yet still able to write. (Since superseded: opencode now maps every
read-only role — `explore` included — to its read-only `plan` agent, so the
role/agent split the fix relied on no longer arises.)

## Clean up sessions

Finished runs leave their tmux sessions behind; eighteen had accumulated by the
end of the afternoon, which reads as "stuck" when it is merely untidy. `sonata
gc` kills the finished ones.

===== FILE 44 docs/guide/adding-a-harness.md =====
# Adding a harness

The adapter boundary is the extension point. A new harness means one new file,
registration in two places, and tests:

1. **`src/adapters/<name>.ts`** — export a `HarnessAdapter`. The interface is
   in [`src/adapters/types.ts`](https://github.com/zhihaohong52/sonata/blob/main/src/adapters/types.ts);
   [`opencode.ts`](https://github.com/zhihaohong52/sonata/blob/main/src/adapters/opencode.ts)
   is the smallest example,
   [`codex.ts`](https://github.com/zhihaohong52/sonata/blob/main/src/adapters/codex.ts)
   the most complete. You implement:
   - `name`, `versionCommand`, `supportedVersions`, `pathPrepend` — identity,
     and the probe sonata runs to read the installed version
   - `plan(input)` → a `LaunchPlan`: the bash `script`, whether the harness is
     `interactive`, and `effortHonoured` (required — whether the plan passes a
     pinned `<key>@<effort>` level through). Optional on the plan:
     `canWriteReport` (false when this configuration cannot write `report.md`
     at all) and `silentUntilExit` (true when nothing reaches the pane until
     the run exits)
   - `canPromptForApproval` — whether the harness can stop and ask a human
   - `promptPatterns` / `describePrompt` — how a pending approval looks
   - `approveKeys` — the tmux key sequences that answer one
   - `usage(query)` — required: the tokens a finished run spent, read from the
     harness's own store, or `unobservable` with a reason. Never guessed, never
     zero
   - optional: `health(env)` — runtime checks beyond "is it installed";
     `update` — how `sonata init` offers to bring the harness up to date;
     `fallbackReportFile` — a file the harness writes its own final message to,
     used as a report fallback before the pane
2. **[`src/adapters/index.ts`](https://github.com/zhihaohong52/sonata/blob/main/src/adapters/index.ts)** — register it.
3. **[`src/config.ts`](https://github.com/zhihaohong52/sonata/blob/main/src/config.ts)** — add the name to `KNOWN_HARNESSES`.
4. **`tests/adapters/<name>.test.ts`** — follow an existing adapter's tests.

Optionally, [`src/detect.ts`](https://github.com/zhihaohong52/sonata/blob/main/src/detect.ts)
for `sonata init` discovery. It probes opencode, pi, codex (via `codex
app-server`'s `model/list`) and reasonix; the `claude` harness is the host and
is never offered for discovery. Note the id shape — opencode, pi and reasonix
take `provider/model` ids, while codex takes a bare id.

**Probe the real binary before you write the adapter.** Every adapter bug found
so far was invisible in the documentation and obvious on the first real run:
OpenCode silently eating a positional argument, codex rejecting a flag that its
own `exec` accepts, both harnesses printing approval prompts that matched none
of the patterns written for them. If you claim a harness prints something,
capture it into `tests/fixtures/panes/` and test against that.
===== FILE 45 docs/guide/alerts.md =====
# Alerts

Sonata can run a command of your choosing when something needs your attention
— an OpenCode Go account hit its cap, every account is capped, a model is
blocked by an account setting, the daily budget is spent — and once a day with
a short digest. The command receives the message on standard input, so it can
be anything that sends text: a Telegram bot script, `mail`, a webhook `curl`.

Alerts are **off by default**. They are sent by the router (`sonata serve`),
never from the request path: nothing here can slow or break a routed request.

## Turning them on

```toml
# ~/.config/sonata/sonata.toml  (the machine config)
[alerts]
enabled = true
command = ["/usr/local/bin/tg-send"]   # argv; the message arrives on stdin
daily_digest = "08:30"                  # optional, local time
```

Or from the shell, which uses the same safe writer as the dashboard's Settings
view (see [Console](console.md#sonata-config)):

```bash
sonata config set alerts.command '["/usr/local/bin/tg-send"]'
sonata config set alerts.enabled true
```

The `[alerts]` table is read from the **machine** `sonata.toml`, and re-read on
every pass, so toggling a flag applies within about a minute with no restart.
An unknown key under `[alerts]` is refused at load, so a typo such as
`enabeld` cannot read as "alerts off".

## Keys

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `false` | Master switch. Nothing is sent, and nothing is recorded as sent, while it is off |
| `command` | `[]` | The program and its arguments, as a list of strings. **Not a shell command line**: it is run as given, with no shell, so no quoting, pipes or `$VAR` expansion. Empty means nothing to send (the router logs this once) |
| `account_capped` | `true` | An account hit its 5-hour, weekly or monthly cap |
| `account_recovered` | `true` | A capped account is serving again |
| `all_accounts_capped` | `true` | Every OpenCode Go account is capped; subagents fall back to Claude |
| `model_blocked` | `true` | An account setting stops a model (OpenCode Go's privacy toggle or region requirement) and the router had to fall past it |
| `budget_reached` | `true` | `[budget] daily_usd` was reached for the UTC day |
| `daily_digest` | unset | `HH:MM`; send the digest once a day at that time |
| `min_interval_minutes` | `30` | The least time between two messages of the same kind. Values above `360` are treated as `360` (logged once) |

The five event flags apply only once `enabled = true`; they all default to on,
so enabling alerts subscribes you to every kind, and you switch off the ones you
do not want.

## What the command receives

The message is plain text on the command's **standard input** — one short
sentence for an event, for example:

```
primary hit its weekly cap. Calls move to ucha1.
ucha1 is serving again.
Every OpenCode Go account is capped. Subagents fall back to Claude.
Daily budget reached: $25.10 of $25.00 used (2026-10-29).
```

Nothing is appended to the argv, and no environment variable carries the text.
The command must exit 0 to count as delivered. It gets 20 seconds, then is
killed (SIGKILL). Its standard output is discarded; the first part of its
standard error is kept for the log line when it fails.

For Telegram, a small wrapper that reads stdin and posts it with the bot API is
all `command` needs to name.

## What keeps it from flooding you

- **A quiet start.** The first pass after `sonata serve` starts (and the first
  after alerts were switched off and on again) only *records* the events that
  already exist as sent. Restarting the router, or enabling alerts during an
  ongoing cap, does not replay history.
- **Each event is sent once.** Event ids are deterministic and the ids already
  sent are kept (the last 500) in `~/.config/sonata/alerts-state.json`. A cap
  that outlives the event window does not re-announce itself while it lasts; an
  account is announced again only after it recovers. A privacy block that the
  router re-detects every hour is announced at most once per 24 hours.
- **A minimum interval per kind.** `min_interval_minutes` spaces messages of the
  same kind. An event held back by it is not lost: it goes out when the interval
  passes, unless it is by then more than six hours old, in which case it is
  dropped. A six-hour-old "capped" is noise.
- **Failure backs off.** If the command fails, the router logs the reason and
  waits 5 minutes before trying again; unsent events wait with it.
- **It never blocks routing.** The loop runs on its own timer once a minute,
  one pass at a time, and every error is caught and logged. A `sonata.toml` that
  will not parse pauses alerts (logged once) rather than disabling them.

## Daily digest

Set `daily_digest = "HH:MM"` for a once-a-day summary: the console's one-line
verdict followed by each account's weekly percentage.

```
Sonata daily digest
All OpenCode Go accounts serving: primary at 21% of week, ucha1 at 8% of week (estimated).
primary: 21% of week
ucha1: 8% of week
```

The time is **local time of the `sonata serve` process** (its `TZ`), and the
digest is sent once per local calendar day, at the first pass at or after that
time. It needs `enabled = true` and a `command`, but not any event flag. It is
not sent on the router's very first pass ever if that pass is already past the
time, and not when the router (re)starts more than an hour after the time
without having sent that day's digest — sonata would rather skip a digest than
announce a stale one. A failed send is retried after the 5-minute backoff.

> `sonata config set alerts.daily_digest` and the parser currently describe the
> value as "UTC `HH:MM`" in their error text. The sender uses local time; set the
> time you want to see it in the timezone the router runs in.

## Events

These are the kinds that can be sent. Other console events (a request rejected,
a call that fell past a candidate, a subagent run finishing or failing) appear in
the dashboard's Feed but never trigger a message.

| Kind | Sent when |
|---|---|
| `account_capped` | An OpenCode Go account's request was refused with a usage-limit 429 (the window it names is in the message) |
| `account_recovered` | That account served a request again |
| `all_accounts_capped` | Every OpenCode Go account is capped at once |
| `model_blocked` | A candidate was refused with an account-setting 400 (`trains on request data`, `requires Global regions`) — the message names the setting that clears it. Conversation-shape 400s are not alerts |
| `budget_reached` | Priced spend for the UTC day reached `[budget] daily_usd` from the **machine** config |

## Checking it works

```bash
sonata config get alerts.enabled
sonata config get alerts.command
```

Then watch the router's log (`sonata serve` output) for lines beginning
`alerts:`: `alerts: sent account_capped`, `alerts: command failed for … — retrying in 5 min`,
or `alerts: enabled but [alerts] command is empty — nothing to send`.

To test the command itself, run it by hand with a message on stdin:

```bash
echo "sonata test message" | /usr/local/bin/tg-send
```

## See also

- [Console](console.md): the dashboard Feed shows every event, alerted or not.
- [OpenCode Go accounts and limits](../opencode-go-limits.md): what a cap is and how the router reacts.
===== FILE 46 docs/guide/codex-subscription.md =====
# Using a ChatGPT (Codex) subscription with sonata

Verified end to end on 2026-08-20 against codex-cli 0.147.0, LiteLLM 1.82.3,
a ChatGPT Plus account, and `gpt-5.6-luna`. Sonata now pins its own LiteLLM
(1.98.0); the dated notes below say what held when they were measured.

A `codex login` credential is **ChatGPT OAuth**, not an OpenAI API key. That
distinction decides everything below, and getting it wrong produces errors that
look like a missing key when nothing is missing.

## The credential

`~/.codex/auth.json` holds:

```
auth_mode: chatgpt
OPENAI_API_KEY: None
tokens.{access_token, refresh_token, id_token, account_id}
```

The access token is a JWT with `aud: ["https://api.openai.com/v1"]` and a
`chatgpt_plan_type` claim. The audience is misleading — see below.

## What the token can and cannot reach

Probed directly with curl:

| Endpoint | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `GET api.openai.com/v1/models` | 403 `Missing scopes: api.model.read` |
| `POST api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions` | **429 `insufficient_quota`** |
| `POST api.openai.com/v1/responses` | 403 `Missing scopes: api.responses.write` |
| `POST chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses` | **200, streams normally** |

The 429 is the informative one: the token **authenticated and passed scope
checks**, then hit billing. A ChatGPT subscription is not API credit. The
metered `api.openai.com` API is a separate, separately-billed product.

**Therefore `base_url = "https://api.openai.com/v1"` can never work for a
ChatGPT-OAuth credential**, no matter how the key is plumbed. The correct base
is `https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex`, the Responses wire API, and
**streaming is mandatory** — a non-streamed request returns
`{"detail":"Stream must be set to true"}`.

The backend also validates entitlement per model: `gpt-5.6-luna` is accepted,
while `gpt-5.3-codex-spark` returns *"not supported when using Codex with a
ChatGPT account."*

## Route 1 — the codex harness (simplest, works today)

Runs the real `codex` CLI, which already speaks all of the above.

```toml
[models."gpt-5.6-luna"]
harness = "codex"
id = "gpt-5.6-luna"

[tiers.code]
simple  = ["gpt-5.6-luna@xhigh"]
complex = ["gpt-5.6-luna@xhigh"]
```

`simple` and `complex` are required lists; `normal` is optional. The `@xhigh`
suffix pins the reasoning-effort level — a bare candidate is refused at load
when the catalog holds the model at any level (see
[Configuration](configuration.md)).

`sonata sync`, then dispatch. Verified: `codex exec -m 'gpt-5.6-luna' -s
workspace-write` completed a real repository task, exit 0.

Note `sonata doctor` will report `key source: codex: no key`. That refers to the
**native** gateway and is irrelevant here — the harness uses codex CLI's own
auth. Note also that `config.models` is resolved before `config.native.models`
([`src/commands/run.ts`](https://github.com/zhihaohong52/sonata/blob/main/src/commands/run.ts)),
so adding a `[models]` entry reroutes an
existing agent without regenerating it or restarting Claude Code.

## Route 2 — the native path (foreign model inside Claude Code's own loop)

LiteLLM ships a first-class `chatgpt` provider that handles this correctly:
`CHATGPT_API_BASE` is already `https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex`, its
`CHATGPT_CLIENT_ID` is the same OAuth app codex uses, it forces `stream:true`
and `store:false`, sends `ChatGPT-Account-Id`, and **refreshes the token
automatically** (`_refresh_tokens`, expiry check with skew).

Working LiteLLM config — note there is **no `api_base` and no `api_key`**; the
provider supplies both:

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: gpt-5.6-luna
    litellm_params:
      model: chatgpt/gpt-5.6-luna
    model_info:
      mode: responses          # REQUIRED — see below
```

Credentials come from `$CHATGPT_TOKEN_DIR/auth.json` (default
`~/.config/litellm/chatgpt/`), in a **flattened** form — codex nests these under
`tokens`:

```json
{"access_token":"…","refresh_token":"…","id_token":"…",
 "expires_at":<jwt exp>,"account_id":"…"}
```

Verified: an Anthropic `/v1/messages` request with `"stream": true` streamed
`NATIVE-STREAM-OK` back through LiteLLM from the subscription.

### `mode: responses` is required

Without it LiteLLM takes the chat-completions path and POSTs to the bare
`backend-api/codex/` URL, which serves the ChatGPT **web app**. The reply is a
Cloudflare "Enable JavaScript and cookies to continue" HTML page, which surfaces
as an opaque `ChatgptException`. This is a configuration error, not bot
detection — identical requests via curl and httpx both succeed.

### Non-streaming calls fail — harmless for Claude Code

With `mode: responses`, a **non-streaming** request fails:

```
ChatgptException - Unknown items in responses API response: []
```

Root cause is upstream and not in the chatgpt provider: the Codex backend sends
`response.completed` with `output: []` and delivers items in preceding
`response.output_item.done` events, which LiteLLM's Responses→ChatCompletions
bridge never accumulates
(`completion_extras/litellm_responses_transformation/transformation.py:540`).

**Streaming clients bypass that bridge entirely**, building content from
`response.output_text.delta`. Claude Code always streams, so this never fires in
normal use. What does break: non-streaming callers — health checks, token
counting, `stream:false` probes.

Upstream: [BerriAI/litellm#25429](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/25429).
As of 2026-08-20 it had been open since 2026-04-09, fix PR
[#31332](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/31332) was still unmerged,
no stable release contained it, and it reproduced on 1.82.3 here.

## How sonata implements Route 2

Configure it by marking the gateway — nothing else is needed:

```toml
[native.gateways."codex"]
auth = "codex-oauth"

[models."gpt-5.6-luna"]
gateway = "codex"
id = "gpt-5.6-luna"
# context_window = 128000   # optional; this is the default
```

`base_url` is not needed, and naming another one is refused: a config naming
the metered API would describe a gateway that can never authenticate. `sonata
init` writes this form by itself when `codex login` used a ChatGPT account.

A sonata-initiated login identifies itself to OpenAI as the Codex CLI. This is
not new behavior: LiteLLM's own Codex provider already makes that identification
on every native Codex request. It is simply a more visible position now that
sonata's own UI starts the login.

What each piece does:

- **`src/config.ts`** parses `auth`, defaulting to `api-key` so existing configs
  are unaffected, and supplies `CODEX_OAUTH_BASE_URL` for codex-oauth.
- **`src/native/litellm.ts`** emits `model: chatgpt/<id>` with
  `model_info.mode: responses` and **no** `api_base`/`api_key` — passing either
  would override the provider and break it.
- **`src/native/codex-auth.ts`** flattens `~/.codex/auth.json` into the record
  LiteLLM reads, deriving `expires_at` from the JWT.
- **`src/commands/serve.ts`** writes that record 0600 into its own temp
  directory and sets `CHATGPT_TOKEN_DIR`, then removes it on stop.
- **`src/commands/doctor.ts`** reports the credential as a subscription rather
  than telling the user to add a key that would be ignored.

Verified end to end: an Anthropic `/v1/messages` streaming request to
`sonata serve`'s router returned `"text": "OK"` from `gpt-5.6-luna`.

### Which login a gateway reads

`credential_source` on `[native.gateways."<name>"]` chooses the store a
gateway authenticates from:

- `sonata` — a login per gateway name, in sonata's own store
  (`sonata auth login <gateway>`).
- `codex` — the credential `codex login` wrote to `~/.codex/auth.json`.
  Refused with `auth = "api-key"` (that is a subscription, not a bearer key)
  and with `copilot-oauth` (Copilot logins come only from opencode).
- `opencode` — opencode's store: its `openai` entry for `codex-oauth`, its
  `github-copilot` entry for `copilot-oauth`.
- absent — a ChatGPT gateway reads codex's login when there is one, else
  opencode's; a Copilot gateway reads opencode's, as it does with
  `credential_source = "opencode"`. On an `api-key` gateway the default
  reads sonata's key store first, then opencode's.

LiteLLM holds one ChatGPT and one Copilot credential per process, so two
gateways of one OAuth kind that resolve to different logins cannot both be
served. Sonata drops every gateway of that kind — their models answer a typed
502 naming the gateways and projects, and the rest of the config keeps
working — and `sonata doctor` warns, naming both. Point them at one
credential.

### The credential must not outlive serve

`serve` runs until killed, so its signal handlers *are* its normal exit path.
Without them `stop()` never runs and the temp directory survives — carrying the
generated master key and, for a codex-oauth gateway, the ChatGPT credential. One
such token was found in the system temp directory during development. `cli.ts`
now stops the handle on SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP, and `run.ts` retains the handle
it used to discard for auto-started serves.

## opencode's OAuth logins

opencode stores two OAuth credentials beside its API keys, and neither is a
bearer key:

| Entry | Value | What it actually is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openai` | JWT, `client_id: app_EMoamEEZ73f0CkXaXp7hrann` | The **same** ChatGPT subscription credential codex holds — same OAuth app. As an `api_key` it 429s. |
| `github-copilot` | opaque `gho_…` | A GitHub OAuth token. Must be exchanged at `api.github.com/copilot_internal/v2/token` for a short-lived Copilot key. |

`opencodeKeys()` is therefore **right** to skip them — it resolves API keys, and
these are not API keys. The bug was that they were then invisible, so `doctor`
reported "no key" for a gateway whose credential was sitting on disk. They are
now read by dedicated readers instead:

- `readOpencodeChatGptOAuth` flattens the `openai` entry into the same record
  `readCodexOAuth` produces, **after checking `client_id`** — another OpenAI
  OAuth grant would fail confusingly inside LiteLLM's chatgpt provider.
- `readChatGptOAuth` prefers codex and falls back to opencode, so
  `auth = "codex-oauth"` works for a machine that only has opencode.
- `readCopilotToken` reads the `github-copilot` entry for the
  `copilot-oauth` gateway kind.

### `auth = "copilot-oauth"`

```toml
[native.gateways."copilot"]
auth = "copilot-oauth"
```

Emits `model: github_copilot/<id>` with no `api_base`/`api_key` and **no** mode
override — Copilot speaks chat-completions, so the Responses bridge that
codex-oauth needs does not apply. `serve` writes the GitHub token to
`access-token` in its temp directory and sets `GITHUB_COPILOT_TOKEN_DIR`;
LiteLLM performs the exchange and caches the Copilot key itself.

**opencode's token usually cannot be used.** Measured on a real machine: the
stored `gho_` token carries scope **`read:user` only** — both the `access` and
`refresh` fields are the same token — so GitHub answers the exchange with

```
403 Forbidden — https://api.github.com/copilot_internal/v2/token
```

LiteLLM then drops the deployment and carries on, and the next request fails as
`no healthy deployments for this model`, naming neither the token nor the scope.
So sonata checks the scope before offering Copilot at all: `init` prints a line
and omits its models, and `doctor` fails the check with the reason. The check
asks GitHub (scopes are not in the opaque token) and **fails closed**, so an
offline machine simply does not offer Copilot rather than offering it wrongly.

To actually use `copilot-oauth`, the token must carry the `copilot` scope —
LiteLLM's own device-code login produces one, writing it to its token
directory.

**Claude models are available:** Copilot serves Claude models, as do other
configured gateways. A configured key routes to its gateway; only an
unconfigured `claude-*` name is passed directly to Anthropic.

**opencode writes `expires: 0`** on the Copilot entry, meaning "does not
expire". Read literally that reports a working token as expired since 1970.

**LiteLLM's output is now inherited** by `serve`. A per-model startup failure
appears only there; discarding it is what made the 403 above surface as an
unrelated-looking "no healthy deployments".
===== FILE 47 docs/guide/commands.md =====
# Commands

Every `sonata` command, grouped by what you would reach for it to do. A
mistyped command suggests the nearest real one.

## Setting up

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `sonata init` | Set up sonata in this project (interactive). Every prompt has a flag for unattended use: `--yes`, `--providers`, `--models`, `--roles`, `--config-scope`, `--scope`, `--routing`, `--guidance`, `--credential-source`; `--repropose-tiers` re-ranks from the catalog, discarding a hand-tuned order; `--prune` removes stale generated agents |
| `sonata` / `sonata tui` | Open the configuration UI. `sonata status`, `sonata usage`, `sonata agents` and `sonata init` open it at their own screen when run in a terminal |
| `sonata agents [--list] [--json]` | Every generated tier agent, what each ranked candidate resolves to, its context window, and whether the alias carries `[1m]`. In a terminal it is also the editor: re-rank a tier without walking the whole wizard |
| `sonata sync [--prune]` | Regenerate agent files from `sonata.toml` and install the `/sonata*` slash commands beside them; `--prune` removes stale generated agents |
| `sonata doctor [--json]` | Check tmux, harnesses, auth and versions, the permission hook, tier routing, model rankings, catalog coverage and freshness, and more; `--json` prints the same checks as structured output |
| `sonata reset [--global] [--yes]` | Remove sonata's configuration and generated files at one scope — the config, the generated agents, the loop skill, the CLAUDE.md block, and the routing env/hooks/allow-list. Keeps your gateway keys, the usage ledger and the caches, and shows the full plan before touching anything |
| `sonata upgrade` | Install the latest published release with `npm install -g`. A development install (`npm link`) is refused and told to `git pull && npm run build` instead. Run `sonata restart` afterwards so the router runs the new version |
| `sonata --version` (`-v`) | The running version and the directory it ran from — how you tell which install answered |

## Credentials and catalogs

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `sonata auth list\|add <gateway>\|remove <gateway>\|login <gateway>` | Manage native-path gateway keys, kept in sonata's own key store. `add` reads the key from the terminal or stdin, never argv; `login` runs the OAuth flow for `codex` and `github-copilot` |
| `sonata auth trust <gateway> <host>\|untrust <gateway> <host>\|trust-list` | Bind a stored key to the hosts it may be sent to. A key is only ever sent to a host bound to its gateway name: the provider's own endpoint, a host you confirmed with `trust`, or the machine config's own URL for that name. `sonata init` binds the URLs typed in its run; `sonata auth add` binds nothing from a config. Anything else needs an explicit `trust` (a host includes its port when one is set; a plain-http loopback host such as `localhost:8000` can be trusted this way too). `sonata doctor` fails a gateway pointing somewhere unbound, naming the config and the command |
| `sonata catalog [update]` | Show the cached catalogs' age, or refresh them: the Artificial Analysis model rankings (needs a stored `artificialanalysis` key), models.dev pricing, and the auto-route decision-model scores. `sonata init` refreshes on its own when a discovered model is missing; `sonata doctor` warns when a cache goes stale |
| `sonata litellm install\|status` | Install or report sonata's own pinned LiteLLM. `status` answering `not-required` is healthy — no gateway in this config routes through it |

## The native router

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `sonata serve [--daemon]` | Run the router (and its LiteLLM child, when a gateway needs one); `--daemon` detaches. Its web UI is at `http://localhost:4100/` by default (`[native.ports] router`) |
| `sonata restart` | Replace the router without cutting a request: the new router starts first and takes the port, the old one finishes every request it is answering (up to 15 minutes) and exits, and a running LiteLLM is reused when its model list and login are unchanged. Refuses to replace a router started from a different sonata install (a development build, a worktree) unless `--force`. Use this rather than killing the router by hand |
| `sonata route auto\|manual [--global]` | Route each session for its lifetime via hooks, keeping Remote Control. `auto` is what `sonata init` offers |
| `sonata route on\|off\|status [--global]` | Route every plain `claude` session in the project (or, with `--global`, every project) through the router |
| `sonata code` | Launch a single routed Claude Code session without writing any settings, starting the router if needed (passes `claude` arguments through). Most setups use `sonata route auto` and plain `claude` instead |
| `sonata status [--session <id>\|--all] [--global]` | Whether the router is up and on which port, then recent alias → candidate served → tokens → failed attempts decisions from the ledger |
| `sonata usage [--since 7d] [--by model\|role\|tier\|route\|effort\|gateway\|lane\|session\|project] [--session <id>] [--project <dir>] [--json]` | Tokens and cost from the ledger — native requests as the router saw them, and dispatch runs read from each harness's own store once they finish (`--by lane` splits the two). Unpriced volume is reported separately, never folded into the total |
| `sonata limits [--json]` | How much of each OpenCode Go account's allowance is used, per 5-hour/weekly/monthly window, with each window's top contributing models and an estimate of when it frees up. Computed from the ledger at OpenCode's list prices, so the numbers are **estimates**; set `plan = "go-plus"` on a gateway on the larger plan. See [opencode-go-limits](../opencode-go-limits.md) |

## The console

See [Console](console.md) for each in full.

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `sonata dashboard [--url-only]` | Print the browser login link for the dashboard (`?k=` carries the sign-in secret). Opens nothing; needs the router to have run once |
| `sonata dashboard set-password [--user <name>] [--random]` | Set a username + password login for the dashboard (default user `ucha`; min 12 characters; read from stdin, no echo on a terminal; `--random` generates one and prints it once). Stored hashed in `~/.config/sonata/ui-users.json` (0600) |
| `sonata top` | A live terminal screen of accounts, ladders, runs and the latest calls (keys `q` `a` `l` `r` `e` `s`, up/down). Piped, prints one snapshot |
| `sonata why [request-id\|last]` | The plain-language explanation of one routed request (default: the newest); exit 1 if none matches |
| `sonata config get <path>` / `set <path> <value>` | Read or change one setting in the machine `sonata.toml` through the console's safe writer; exit 1 with the reason when refused |
| `sonata enable <gateway\|model>` / `sonata disable <gateway\|model>` | Switch an account or a model in or out of every tier ladder and print which tiers gain or lose a candidate. Short names (`ucha1`) work when unambiguous |
| `sonata statusline [--color]` | One short routing segment for a Claude Code status line. `sonata-statusline` is the same command without the CLI start-up cost |

`sonata status`, `sonata usage` and `sonata limits` open with a one-line
verdict on the OpenCode Go accounts.

## The dispatch lane

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `sonata dispatch (--tier <role>-<tier> \| --model <key>) [--task-file <path>] "<task>"` | Blocking harness dispatch with ranked fallback — what a tier agent runs when every native route fails. Prints `dispatched <id> model=<m>` as each candidate launches, before blocking, so a caller cut off by its own tool timeout already holds the id and resumes with `sonata wait <id>` |
| `sonata run --role <role> --model <key> --task-file <path> [--json]` | Launch a run in the background and print its id |
| `sonata wait <id>` | Resume a running or approved run and block until its next state — finished, needs approval, or stalled |
| `sonata approve <id> (--yes\|--no)` | Answer a pending approval. Deliberately not allow-listed: every call goes through the permission prompt, so approvals reach a human |
| `sonata tail <id>` | A human view of a run's progress |
| `sonata log <id>` | Print what a run printed |
| `sonata verify <id> [--model <key>]` | Verify a completed run |
| `sonata runs [--json]` | List this project's dispatch runs, with state, whether each wrote a report, and `unchanged` for a finished run that left the worktree as it found it |
| `sonata gc` | Kill finished tmux sessions |

Any live run can also be watched directly: `tmux attach -t sonata-<id>` (add
`-r` for read-only).
===== FILE 48 docs/guide/configuration.md =====
# Configuration

```toml
# sonata.toml
[models."flash"]
gateway = "acme"                    # native route: this key resolves through the router
id = "deepseek-v4-flash-0731"

[models."kimi-k3"]
harness = "opencode"                # harness route: sonata dispatch --tier/--model falls back to this
id = "openrouter/kimi-k3"

[native.gateways."acme"]
base_url = "https://gateway.acme.example/v1"

[tiers.code]
simple  = ["flash", "kimi-k3"]       # tried in this order; a cooling-down candidate is skipped
normal  = ["flash", "kimi-k3"]       # optional; absent is valid, empty is refused
complex = ["kimi-k3", "flash"]

[run]
tail_window_seconds     = 20     # how long `sonata tail` blocks per call
stall_timeout_seconds   = 120    # silence before a run is reported STALLED
run_timeout_seconds     = 1800   # hard cap; the run is killed at this point
dispatch_window_seconds = 540    # how long `sonata wait` blocks before giving up
```

A `[models."<key>"]` entry can carry `gateway`/`id` (native), `harness`/`harness_id`
(dispatch fallback), or both — one model, two routes. `sonata init` writes this
shape for you; see [Using it](getting-started.md#using-it) for how the generated agents use it.

A native model that answers `Function tools with reasoning_effort are not supported
… use /v1/responses` (seen from `gpt-6.1-sol` and `gpt-6-astra` on an
OpenAI-compatible gateway) needs `api = "responses"` on its entry. That sends it
to the gateway's `/responses` endpoint instead of `/chat/completions`. It only
applies to an `api-key` gateway reached through LiteLLM, and is refused anywhere
else. `sonata init` keeps the line when it rewrites the file, and adds it itself
for a model models.dev says is served only there (OpenCode Go's GPT models, for
one); `sonata doctor` names any such model that lacks it.

`api = "google"` does the same for a model served only on Google's own
protocol — OpenCode Go's Gemini models. OpenCode Go serves that protocol only at
`https://opencode.ai/inference/go/v1`, not the older `…/zen/go/v1`; `sonata
init` now writes the first, and `sonata doctor` tells you if a gateway needs
switching.

## Where sonata.toml lives

Sonata looks for a config in three places, in order, and uses exactly one:

1. `./sonata.toml` — the current repository
2. `sonata.toml` in a linked git worktree's main checkout, when the worktree
   has none of its own
3. `~/.config/sonata/sonata.toml` — the machine

A project config wins outright; it is never merged with the machine one. So a
repository with its own `sonata.toml` sees only that file, and adding one
repo-specific model means copying the machine entries alongside it.

`sonata init` asks which you want, and writes the agents to match — project
agents into `./.claude/agents/`, machine agents into `~/.claude/agents/`, where
Claude Code offers them in every repository. Use `--config-scope project|global`
to skip the prompt.

`sonata doctor` prints the config path it actually used.

Roles live in `roles/*.md` and are owned by sonata rather than the harness, so
"review" means the same thing whichever model performs it — which is what makes
comparing two models' reviews meaningful.

Four roles ship: `code`, `review`, `explore` and `plan`. The last three are
**read-only**, enforced by the harness rather than by the prompt alone — a
read-only sandbox on codex, a tool allowlist on pi, a read-only agent on
opencode. The strength of that guarantee differs per harness; see
[Permission modes](permission-modes.md).

Each role chooses its own ranked model list, per tier, through `[tiers.<role>]`.
`simple` and `complex` are required; `normal` is optional. An absent `normal`
list is valid: no `<role>-normal` agent is generated, and a `sonata-<role>-normal`
alias resolves to nothing. A present-but-empty list is refused at parse time.
The older flat `[generate.roles]`/`[generate.native]` pair is
migrated automatically the next time you run `sonata init` (a config still in
that shape parses fine in the meantime — `sonata doctor` just points at
`init` to migrate it).

A tier candidate may pin a reasoning-effort level: `"gpt-5.6-luna@xhigh"`.
The level is one of `default`, `none`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`,
`xhigh`, `max`. `default` means run the model as it ships — no
`reasoning_effort` is sent at all. The level belongs to the *slot*, not the
model — the same model may sit in `simple` at `high` and in `complex` at
`max`. `sonata init` ranks every
level Artificial Analysis has scored for a model as its own row, because for
the current generation the level is often the larger lever: GPT-5.6 Luna at
`max` out-scores GPT-5.6 Terra at every level below `max`, at an eighth of
the cost per task.

**A bare candidate whose model the catalog holds at any effort level is
refused when the config loads** — a family of one counts, because its single
row is still a level to pin. Ranked bare, it is scored at the model's
default row (usually its highest level) and dispatched with no level at all,
so what the ranking promised and what runs are different models. The error
names the candidate, its levels and its default; `sonata init` re-ranks
every tier with levels. With no catalog cache the check cannot run, and
`sonata doctor` says so.

**What a pinned level actually does.** A native tier agent's requests carry
`reasoning_effort` at that level, recorded on each ledger row — `sonata usage
--by effort` breaks spend down by it. A `sonata dispatch` run passes it to the
harness: `-c model_reasoning_effort` on codex, `--variant` on opencode,
`--thinking` on pi (where `none` becomes pi's own `off`), and in the model name
for the claude harness, which routes back through sonata's router. `sonata
dispatch --model <key>@<effort>` takes the same grammar as a tier candidate,
and refuses an unknown level rather than dropping it.

Where sonata has no way to set a level — reasonix today, because it was not
installed on the machine the others were probed on — the run goes ahead at the
harness default and its report opens with `[effort xhigh not honoured: sonata
has no effort control for reasonix]`. That is a note, not a failure: the report
is still trusted, and the run is not marked degraded. Effort is a preference,
unlike a permission mode, which sonata refuses rather than quietly downgrades.

One limit worth stating: sonata can see that it sent the level, not that the
model applied it. A gateway without an effort control drops the field silently,
and `opencode run` accepts a `--variant` a model does not publish without
complaining. The evidence a level did anything is cost per task moving with it
in `sonata usage`.

Run `sonata sync` after editing the config; Claude Code picks up the
generated agents automatically.

## Auto-routed tiers

Opt in per project by adding:

```toml
[auto_route]
classifier = "jev"
min_confidence = 0.5
```

`classifier` must be `"jev"`; `min_confidence` is optional and must be between 0 and 1 (the default is `0.5`).

Jev is asked wherever `base_url` points — any http(s) URL speaking its API:

- TypeSafe directly (the default, `https://api.typesafe.ai`). Store the key with `sonata auth add typesafe`.
- OpenRouter (`base_url = "https://openrouter.ai/api"`), using the key your `openrouter` gateway already uses (`sonata auth add openrouter`, or one opencode holds). No TypeSafe account is needed.
- A self-hosted `jev-compatible-server`, e.g. `base_url = "http://localhost:8000"`. A local server usually needs no key, and then it works as it is. A keyed one needs no trust in your machine config, which is trusted by definition; in a project config it needs `sonata auth trust auto-route localhost:8000` (the host with its port). Any other host takes a key stored with `sonata auth add auto-route`.

The key follows the host and is only ever sent to it: the OpenRouter key goes to `openrouter.ai`, the TypeSafe key to `api.typesafe.ai`. The key is read when each classification is made and is never logged.

```toml
[auto_route]
classifier = "jev"
base_url = "https://openrouter.ai/api"
# model = "typesafe/jev-1.13"            # optional pin; skips selection
min_confidence = 0.5
```

Unless `model` pins one, sonata lists the decision models the URL serves (cached an hour per URL) and takes the one with the highest JevBench capability score — an exact tie goes to the cheaper listed price, and a model JevBench does not score never beats one it does. With nothing scored, it uses `~typesafe/jev-latest` on `openrouter.ai`, `jev-latest` on `api.typesafe.ai`, and sends no `model` field to any other host (the server's default). `model` skips that choice: pin a Jev release with `model = "typesafe/jev-1.13"`, or name any other decision model the URL serves. Run `sonata catalog update` to cache the JevBench scores; `sonata doctor` shows the URL, the key it needs, and the model chosen.

When enabled, `sonata sync` generates a `<role>-auto` agent for each role whose tiers differ. Jev chooses among that role's available `simple`, `normal` and `complex` tiers once per conversation; the selected tier then follows the same ranked native routing path as its explicit tier agent. If the key is missing, the request fails, the task is empty, Jev returns an invalid or low-confidence answer, or the deadline is exceeded, sonata falls back to `normal`, or `complex` when `normal` is unavailable. Use the explicit tier agents when you already know the right tier.

Classifier calls are not charged against `[budget] daily_usd`. `sonata usage --by route` separates auto-routed requests from manual tier requests and reports classifier token volume beside the priced total. Where the response reports a cost (OpenRouter's does), `sonata usage` sums it and shows it apart from the priced total; a decision asked on a loopback URL (`localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`) is recorded as free ($0) even when its response reports no cost, and only a non-loopback decision whose response reports no cost stays unpriced.

## Seeing and changing a ranking

`sonata agents` prints every generated tier agent, what each of its ranked
candidates resolves to, that model's context window, and whether the agent's
alias carries `[1m]`:

```text
code-simple
    1. flash                        acme/deepseek-v4-flash-0731  128K
    2. kimi-k3                      opencode/openrouter/kimi-k3  window unknown  harness only
```

Three things there are invisible in the file itself: what a key actually
resolves to, whether every native candidate clears 1M (which is what decides
the `[1m]` suffix, and it has to hold for *whichever* model answers, not the
best one), and whether a key still names a model at all.

Run it in a terminal and it is also the editor — `enter` re-ranks one list
through the same picker `sonata init` uses, `w` writes and regenerates the
agent files. `--list` prints without the editor, `--json` emits the same rows
for a script.

**A saved ranking is never re-ranked for you.** Upgrading sonata, or
refreshing the catalog, changes what `sonata init` would propose but leaves
your saved order alone. On the ranking board, `r` replaces that list with the
order the catalog suggests now; it is written only when you confirm with
`enter` and `w`, and `←` discards it. `sonata init --repropose-tiers` does the
same for every list at once.

**The `--json` shape changed when effort levels landed.** A row's `key` now
holds the whole candidate, `@effort` included (`acme-big@high`), rather than a
bare key into `[models]`, and a sibling `effort` field carries the level on its
own. A script that fed `key` straight back into a `[models]` lookup needs to
split it — `key` is the candidate, not the model.

It is the only writer of `sonata.toml` besides `sonata init`, and it replaces
the `[tiers]` tables alone: every other byte of your config, including
hand-written `price` entries and `pricing_provider`, is left exactly where it
was. It refuses to write at all if the file changed while the editor was open,
rather than reverting a tier you edited elsewhere.

## Starting over

`sonata reset` removes what `sonata init` wrote at one scope — the config, the
generated agents, the loop skill, the managed `CLAUDE.md` block, and the
routing env, lifecycle hooks, permission hook and tool allow-list from the
settings files. Add `--global` for the machine scope, `--yes` to skip the
confirmation.

It removes **only what sonata wrote**: an agent file you wrote by hand survives,
`permissions.allow` keeps every entry that is not sonata's, and `CLAUDE.md`
loses what is between the sonata markers and nothing else. It **keeps** what is
expensive to recreate — your gateway keys, the usage ledger, the ranking and
pricing caches, and the `.sonata/` run store — and prints that list, so a
reset never silently costs you your credentials or spend history. The full plan
is shown, path by path, before anything is touched.

## Config keys

The whole grammar `sonata.toml` parses. Top-level keys must sit above every
`[table]` header — a bare key after one belongs to that table.

**Top level**

- `schema_version` — integer stamp; the current value is `2` and a newer one
  is refused. Older files are migrated in memory on every load; nothing is
  written back.
- `avoid_gateways` — list of gateway names whose models rank last in every
  tier. Demotion, never exclusion: they stay as last-resort candidates. An
  unknown name is refused, so a typo cannot read as an unused setting.
- `gateway_order` — list of gateway names that breaks ranking *ties* only; a
  gateway left out is neutral. An unknown or repeated name is refused.

**`[budget]`**

- `daily_usd` — positive number of US dollars. It counts priced spend only
  (unpriced volume is reported beside it, never folded in as zero), including
  a `sonata dispatch` run once that run finishes. Both the router and
  `sonata dispatch` refuse at the cap — but a dispatch run cannot be stopped
  midway, so one run can carry spend past it. Subscription-covered work — a
  `codex-oauth`, `copilot-oauth` or Claude `session` gateway, or any gateway
  on a flat-rate plan (see `billing` below) — shows as `$x sub` and never
  counts. A non-positive or non-numeric value is refused
  at parse time; remove the table to run without a cap.

**`[alerts]`** — messages from the router when an account or the budget needs
attention; off by default. Full guide: [Alerts](alerts.md). Read from the
machine config. Unknown keys and non-boolean flags are refused at load.

- `enabled` — `false` by default; nothing is sent while it is off.
- `command` — argv list the message is piped to on standard input (no shell).
- `account_capped`, `account_recovered`, `all_accounts_capped`,
  `model_blocked`, `budget_reached` — per-event switches, each `true` by
  default once `enabled` is on.
- `daily_digest` — optional `HH:MM`; a once-a-day summary, in the local time of
  the `sonata serve` process.
- `min_interval_minutes` — least time between two messages of one kind
  (integer >= 1, default `30`, treated as at most `360`).

**`[ui]`** — the web dashboard (see [Console](console.md)).

- `allowed_hosts` — list of extra `Host` header values the dashboard accepts
  beside loopback, for a reverse proxy or Tailscale name. Exact match on the
  bare host (case-insensitive, port ignored); no wildcards; an IPv6 literal is
  written in brackets (`"[2001:db8::1]"`). Default empty: loopback only.

**`[native.ports]`**

- `router` — port for `sonata serve`'s router (default `4100`).
- `litellm` — port for the managed LiteLLM child (default `4000`).

**`[native.gateways."<name>"]`**

- `base_url` — the endpoint (required on an `api-key` gateway). An OAuth
  gateway cannot point it anywhere but the URL its credential reaches —
  naming the metered OpenAI API on a `codex-oauth` gateway is refused (see
  [Codex subscription auth](codex-subscription.md)); an `auth = "session"`
  gateway accepts only `https://api.anthropic.com`.
- `auth` — `api-key` (default), `codex-oauth`, `copilot-oauth`, or `session`.
- `provider` — one of `openai`, `anthropic`, `gemini`, `deepseek`, `mistral`,
  `groq`, `openrouter`, selecting the wire dialect LiteLLM speaks.
  `wire_format = "openai"|"anthropic"` is the older spelling; `provider` wins
  when both are set. Neither may be set on an OAuth gateway, whose dialect is
  fixed by its auth.
- `credential_source` — `sonata`, `codex`, or `opencode`: which login the
  gateway reads. `codex` is refused with `api-key` and with `copilot-oauth`,
  and `session` cannot set it. See
  [Codex subscription auth](codex-subscription.md#which-login-a-gateway-reads).
- `billing` — `subscription` or `metered`, on an `api-key` gateway only:
  whether it is a flat-rate plan. Subscription work is valued at list but
  never billed per token, so it is reported as covered and left out of
  `[budget]`. Unset, the endpoint decides — see
  [Subscription plans](native-path.md#subscription-plans) — so set it only for
  a plan that shares its pay-as-you-go endpoint (MiniMax, Synthetic, Chutes,
  NanoGPT, Ollama Cloud, Cerebras Code), or to correct sonata. An OAuth or
  `session` gateway cannot set it.
- `plan` — `go` or `go-plus`: which OpenCode Go plan this account is on, so
  `sonata limits` and the console use the right monthly limits. Unset means `go`.
  Refused on OAuth and `session` gateways. See
  [OpenCode Go accounts and limits](../opencode-go-limits.md).
- `price` — rates as below.
- `pricing_provider` — name(s) of the models.dev provider(s) whose rates
  price this gateway's models, instead of hand-written ones. For a plan
  endpoint, `sonata init` proposes the plan's pay-as-you-go sibling (`zai`
  for the GLM Coding Plan), because models.dev lists plans at $0.
- `enabled` — `false` removes every model on this gateway from tier
  candidacy; absent means enabled. It is routing state, so any auth may set
  it, and it survives a `sonata init` rewrite. `enabled = false` removes a
  gateway or model from tier ladders; an explicit `--model` request still
  reaches it.

**`[models."<key>"]`**

- `gateway` — the native route's gateway name; or `harness` — the dispatch
  route's harness (`opencode`, `codex`, `pi`, `reasonix`, `claude`); or both.
- `id` — the upstream model id for `gateway`, the harness-side ref for
  `harness` alone.
- `harness_id` — optional harness-side id when the two differ. Unset, codex
  takes `id` bare, opencode/pi/reasonix take `<gateway>/<id>`, and `claude`
  takes the config key.
- `api = "responses"` — send to the gateway's `/responses` endpoint instead
  of `/chat/completions`; `api = "google"` — send over Google's
  `generateContent` protocol at the gateway's base URL. Only on an `api-key`
  gateway reached through LiteLLM; refused anywhere else.
- `context_window` — tokens, for the native route (default `128000`).
- `price` — rates as below.
- `enabled` — `false` drops this model from tier candidacy; absent means
  enabled. It survives a `sonata init` rewrite. `enabled = false` removes a
  gateway or model from tier ladders; an explicit `--model` request still
  reaches it.

**`price`** (on a model or a gateway) is USD per 1,000,000 tokens: `input`,
`cached_input`, `cache_write`, `output`, each optional; a rate of `0` is a
real price (a free tier). `windows` is an optional array of tables with
`from` and `to` as UTC `HH:MM` plus the same rate keys; evaluated in order,
the first match wins. A rate a window does not set falls back to the flat
rate, so a window setting only `input` still charges the flat `output`. A
window whose `from` equals its `to` is refused.
===== FILE 49 docs/guide/console.md =====
# Console

The console is everything sonata shows you about routing, accounts and
subagents, on four surfaces that read the same data and say the same thing: a
web dashboard served by the router, a live terminal screen (`sonata top`), a
set of plain commands (`sonata why`, `sonata limits`, `sonata status`, …) and a
segment for Claude Code's status line. State is shown visually first (bars,
coloured chips) and in words second.

None of it changes how requests are routed. The console reads the usage ledger
and the router's own state; the only things it can change are the settings
listed under [Changing settings](#changing-settings), and only through the
same safe writer in every case.

Every number is an **estimate** where it concerns an OpenCode Go allowance —
see [OpenCode Go accounts and limits](../opencode-go-limits.md) for how it is
computed and what the router does when an account runs out.

## The web dashboard

`sonata serve` serves the dashboard on the router's port (`http://127.0.0.1:4100/`
unless `[native.ports] router` says otherwise). It is a built web app shipped
inside the package (`dist/ui/`), with its fonts and icons bundled, so it works
offline and adds no runtime dependency to the router.

### Opening it

```bash
sonata dashboard            # prints the login link and a one-line hint
sonata dashboard --url-only # prints only the link, for scripts
```

The link looks like `http://127.0.0.1:4100/?k=<secret>`. Opening it in a
browser trades the secret for a session cookie and redirects to the same
address without `?k=`, so the secret does not stay in the address bar or the
history. The secret is the `ui-token` file `sonata serve` creates at
`~/.config/sonata/ui-token` (mode 0600); `sonata dashboard` only reads it and
exits 1 with a hint if the router has never been started. Treat the link like
the file it came from: print it only in a terminal you are reading.

**Without the cookie the dashboard is read-only, on loopback.** Anyone who can
reach `127.0.0.1` can read every view; changing a setting or killing a run needs
the session. Through a proxy name from `allowed_hosts` even reads need the
session (see [Host check](#reaching-it-through-a-proxy-allowed-hosts)). A wrong or
missing `?k=` is not an error: the page just loads without a session.

The session cookie (`sonata_ui`) is HttpOnly and `SameSite=Strict`, lasts 30
days, and is `Secure` only when the request carries `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`.
Sessions live in the router's memory: **restarting the router signs every
browser out** (open the link again). Every write also needs a per-process CSRF
nonce that the page only receives when it holds a session, and an `Origin`
header, if present, must match the `Host`. The router token that authorises
requests to choose a project is never sent to a browser.

### Signing in with a username and password

The `?k=` link needs a terminal on the router's machine. For a dashboard you
reach by name (see [`allowed_hosts`](#reaching-it-through-a-proxy-allowed-hosts))
set a password once and sign in from any browser:

```bash
sonata dashboard set-password                    # user "ucha"; typed twice, no echo
sonata dashboard set-password --user alice       # another account
echo 'a long passphrase' | sonata dashboard set-password   # piped, for scripts
sonata dashboard set-password --random           # generates a password, prints it once
```

- The password must be at least 12 characters. It is stored as a scrypt hash
  (random salt, N=32768) in `~/.config/sonata/ui-users.json`, mode 0600, written
  atomically; the password itself is never stored. Run the command again for an
  existing user to change their password. Usernames are case-insensitive. The
  router reads the file on every login, so no restart is needed. Sessions that
  are already open stay open until the router restarts or they expire.
- A page with no session shows a sign-in screen when the router refuses its API
  reads (403: any `allowed_hosts` name). A good login sets the same `sonata_ui`
  cookie the `?k=` link does, and the page reloads signed in; the sidebar then
  has a **Sign out** button. On loopback, where reads are open, the page stays
  read-only until you sign in by link or password.
- It is `POST /__sonata/api/login` with `{"username","password"}`
  (`application/json` only, at most 4 KiB; an `Origin`, if present, must match
  the `Host`, and `Sec-Fetch-Site` must be `same-origin` or `none`) and
  `POST /__sonata/api/logout`. A failed login is always `401 {"ok":false}`: it
  never says whether the user exists, and an unknown user costs the same
  scrypt work as a wrong password.
- **Brute-force limits** are kept in the router's memory (a restart clears
  them) and never lock anyone out, so a stranger cannot shut the owner out of
  their own dashboard. Instead the Nth consecutive failed login for a username
  within 15 minutes makes the *next* attempt for that username wait
  min(2^(N-1), 30) seconds (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 30, 30 ...). An attempt that
  arrives during the wait gets `429` with `Retry-After` set to the seconds
  left; it is not verified and does not extend the wait. A correct password
  after the wait always succeeds and resets that username's count. The same
  scheme runs over failures across all usernames, capped at 5 seconds, so the
  owner waits at most 5 seconds while someone is guessing. Attempts are counted
  when they begin, so parallel guesses do not get ahead of the wait. The router
  sees every proxied request from `127.0.0.1`, so there is no per-address
  limit and `X-Forwarded-For` is never trusted; with a long random password
  (`--random` makes 32 characters) guessing is still hopeless at this rate.
- **A password session is tied to its account and password.** `sonata
  dashboard set-password` ends that user's existing password sessions, and so
  does removing the account from `ui-users.json`; other users' sessions and
  `?k=` link sessions are not affected (a link session is bound to `ui-token`,
  not to an account).

A `?k=` pasted onto any other path (such as `/v1/messages?k=…`) is dropped
before the request is logged or forwarded.

### Views

The sidebar has six views, hash-routed
(`#/home`, `#/console`, …). `Ctrl-K` (or `Cmd-K`) opens a command palette to
jump between views, explain the last call, and change theme.

| View | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Home** | The verdict (ok, degraded or down, in one sentence), one tile per OpenCode Go account with its 5-hour, weekly and monthly bars and a capped flag, the busiest ladder, recent events and the running subagents |
| **Console** | Every role and tier ladder, with each candidate as a state chip, and a coding-intelligence chart of every model a tier can reach (Artificial Analysis' coding index where it publishes one; a model it has not scored shows an empty bar, never a guess) |
| **Feed** | Newest-first plain-sentence events with filter chips: All, Problems, Accounts, Subagents, Config |
| **Runs** | Every dispatch run: state, role, model, the account that served it, a transcript tail and the report. A Kill button stops a running one |
| **Explain** | Any recent request told in plain language: who was tried, why each was passed over, who answered and what it cost in tokens |
| **Settings** | Appearance (palette, glass, light/dark; saved in this browser), and the routing settings below |

The ladder chips are the same states `sonata top` and `sonata why` use:
**serving**, **cooling** (the router is skipping it for a while, with the
time left), **capped**, **blocked** (an account setting stops the model, such
as OpenCode Go's privacy setting), **idle** and **not reached**. Each carries a
glyph as well as a colour.

### Changing settings

The Settings view, `sonata config set` and `sonata enable|disable` all call the
same writer (its design is recorded in `docs/internals/configuration.md`),
so they accept the same things and refuse the same things. Through the
dashboard (needs the sign-in link):

- enable or disable a gateway (account) or a model, and set a gateway's `plan`
  (`go` or `go-plus`);
- reorder a tier's ladder (a reorder only: no adding or removing candidates);
- the `[alerts]` toggles, and `[budget] daily_usd`.

Credentials, base URLs and ports are never settable from the console. Two
settings the CLI writes are also refused from the dashboard (403, "not writable
from the dashboard; use `sonata config set`"): `alerts.command`, an argv the
daemon executes, and `ui.allowed_hosts`, which decides who can reach the
dashboard at all. A reorder submitted for a tier that has disabled candidates may
list only the enabled ones: the disabled entries keep their positions. Reordering
a role whose tiers are all the same list applies the order to every tier, so it
stays one list. The router re-reads `sonata.toml` on every request, so a change applies without a
restart.

### Reaching it through a proxy: `allowed_hosts`

The router listens on loopback only, and the dashboard checks the `Host`
header of every request against that, to defeat DNS rebinding. To open it
through a reverse proxy, Tailscale or any other name, list the host:

```toml
[ui]
allowed_hosts = ["sonata.example.com", "[2001:db8::1]"]
```

- Matching is **exact on the bare host**: case-insensitive, port ignored. There
  are **no wildcards and no suffix rule** — `sonata.example.com` does not admit
  `evil-sonata.example.com` or `a.sonata.example.com`.
- An **IPv6 literal is written in brackets**, the way a `Host` header spells it:
  `[2001:db8::1]`.
- Loopback stays allowed; the list only adds to it. An empty list is exactly the
  old loopback-only rule.
- A `Host` header containing a comma (duplicate `Host` headers) is always
  refused.
- Your proxy must pass the original `Host` through (or rewrite it to a listed
  name), and should forward `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` so the cookie is marked
  `Secure`.
- The setting is read from the **machine** `sonata.toml`, re-read per request
  through a 5-second cache, so editing it needs no restart.
- **Forward only `/` and `/__sonata/*`.** The router's proxy surface (`/v1/*`,
  `/__sonata_health`, a `POST /`) answers **only to a loopback `Host`**
  (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`, with the router's port or none) and is
  answered 403 for any other, listed or not, so a DNS-rebinding page or a proxy
  name never reaches the stored gateway keys. This holds even with an empty
  `allowed_hosts`. Point clients at `http://localhost:<port>`.
- **API reads need sign-in on non-loopback hosts.** Every `/__sonata/api/*`
  request under a listed name needs the `sonata_ui` session cookie (403
  otherwise). The page, its static files and the `?k=` login stay reachable
  without one, so you can still sign in. Loopback is unchanged.

`sonata dashboard` always prints a loopback address. To sign in through the
proxy, either use a [username and password](#signing-in-with-a-username-and-password)
or replace the origin of that link with the proxy's and keep `?k=…`. The
list is also settable with `sonata config set ui.allowed_hosts '["sonata.example.com"]'`.

### Polling and caching

The dashboard is a glance, not a ticker. Each view polls on its own slow
schedule (Home and ladders every 15 s, runs every 15 s, feed every 20 s,
catalog every 30 s, an open run every 10 s), and **stops polling when the tab
is hidden or the window has been out of focus for more than a minute**. A page
nobody is looking at costs the router nothing. Elapsed times tick locally.

On the router side the heavy answers (`/console`, `/limits`, `/ladders`,
`/verdict`, `/feed`, `/runs`, `/catalog`) are computed once and reused for 5 s
between viewers, and dropped earlier when new ledger rows arrive or a settings
write lands; the ledger itself is read once per process and advanced by
appended bytes, not re-read per request. A cooldown chip can therefore lag by
up to 5 s. The built files are served with correct types, content-hashed files
as immutable, and `ETag`/`304` for the rest; `HEAD` works for the page and its
files. Every response forbids framing.

## `sonata top`

```bash
sonata top
```

A live, btop-style screen that fits an 80x24 terminal and re-reads every 2 s:
the verdict line, each OpenCode Go account's 5-hour/week/month bars with its
capped flag and when it frees up, the busiest ladder's candidates as chips, the
running runs and the newest routed calls. It computes everything in-process
from the same functions the dashboard uses, so it works with no router running;
when a router is up, `sonata top` also asks it for its ladders every 30 s so
live cooldowns show. Piped (or in CI), it prints one plain-text snapshot and
exits 0.

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `q` | Quit |
| `a` | Focus the accounts panel (press again to go back to the calls) |
| `l` | Cycle the ladders (the busiest is shown first) |
| `r` | Focus the runs panel |
| up / down, `k` / `j` | Select a call |
| `e` | Explain the selected call (the newest if none is selected); `e` or Esc closes |
| `s` | Show the `sonata config`, `enable` and `disable` commands for changing settings |

`sonata top` takes no flags.

## `sonata why`

```bash
sonata why            # the newest request
sonata why last       # the same
sonata why <call-id>  # a specific request
```

Prints the plain-language explanation of one routed request: each candidate
that was tried, why it was passed over ("primary spark rejected: weekly cap"),
and who answered, with time and tokens. The id is a request's call id, as shown
by the dashboard feed and the Explain view. It looks back seven days; exit
code 1 when nothing matches. The text is the same one the dashboard's Explain
view shows.

## `sonata limits`, `sonata status`, `sonata usage`

`sonata limits` is the allowance report described in
[OpenCode Go accounts and limits](../opencode-go-limits.md): one line per Go
account with 5-hour, weekly and monthly percentages and when each window frees
up. `sonata limits --json` returns the same report.

`sonata limits`, `sonata status` and `sonata usage` all **open with the
console's one-line verdict**, coloured by level on a terminal and plain when
piped:

```
● All OpenCode Go accounts serving: primary at 21% of week, ucha1 at 8% of week (estimated).
```

(or "degraded" / "down" with the reason and when a capped account frees up).
`sonata status` and `sonata usage` then show each account's three bars. The
`--json` output of `limits` and `usage` gains an additive `verdict` field. The
verdict is computed from the ledger and the config, so a candidate that is only
*cooling* in the router reads as idle on the command line; the live cooldowns
are on the dashboard and in `sonata top`.

## `sonata config`

```bash
sonata config get alerts.enabled
sonata config set alerts.enabled true
sonata config set alerts.command '["/usr/local/bin/tg-send"]'
sonata config set budget.daily_usd 25
sonata config set native.gateways.opencode-go-ucha1.plan go-plus
sonata config set tiers.code.complex '["kimi-k3","flash"]'
```

Reads or changes one setting in the **machine** `sonata.toml` (never a project
config), through the same writer as the Settings view. Settable paths:

| Path | Value |
|---|---|
| `alerts.enabled`, `alerts.account_capped`, `alerts.account_recovered`, `alerts.all_accounts_capped`, `alerts.model_blocked`, `alerts.budget_reached` | `true` / `false` |
| `alerts.command` | argv as a JSON list of strings |
| `alerts.daily_digest` | `HH:MM` |
| `alerts.min_interval_minutes` | integer >= 1 |
| `ui.allowed_hosts` | JSON list of strings |
| `native.gateways.<name>.enabled`, `models.<key>.enabled` | `true` / `false` |
| `native.gateways.<name>.plan` | `go` or `go-plus` |
| `tiers.<role>.<tier>` | the same candidates, in a new order (a permutation) |
| `budget.daily_usd` | positive number of US dollars |

A value is read as `true`/`false`, then a number, then JSON when it starts with
`[` or `"`, and otherwise as the raw string. `get` prints the value (`(unset)`
when there is none). `set` prints `old -> new`, says "nothing changed" when the
value is already that, and **exits 1 with the validator's message** when it
refuses (an unknown path lists the settable ones; a path naming a credential,
URL or port says those live elsewhere). `sonata config --help` lists the same
paths.

## `sonata enable` / `sonata disable`

```bash
sonata disable ucha1        # take an account out of every ladder
sonata enable ucha1
sonata disable glm-flash    # take one model out
```

Flips the `enabled` flag of a gateway or a model and prints which tier lists
lose or gain a reachable candidate:

```
disabled gateway opencode-go-ucha1 (was enabled)
  code.complex: loses spark@max
  review.simple: loses spark@xhigh
```

**Name resolution.** The name is a gateway name or a model key from
`sonata.toml`, or a short form of one. The first of these rules that matches
anything decides, case-insensitively: the exact name; a name ending in
`-<input>` (`ucha1` finds `opencode-go-ucha1`); one starting with `<input>-`;
one containing `-<input>-`; any substring. If that rule matches **more than one**
name, nothing changes: the candidates are listed and the command exits 1, so a
short form never silently picks the wrong account. No match lists every
gateway and model.

**What `enabled = false` means.** The gateway or model drops out of every tier
ladder when the router resolves one, so it is never tried as a candidate. It is
routing state only: the model keeps its entry, its key and its history, an
**explicit `--model` request still reaches it**, and it survives a
`sonata init` rewrite. A change that would leave a tier with every candidate
disabled is refused (the parser's message, exit 1). Disabling a model whose
gateway is already off reports "no tier changes: its gateway is disabled".

## Inside Claude Code

### The status line segment

```bash
sonata statusline [--color]
```

Prints one short segment for a status line script:

| Output | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sonata: ok` | Every Go account is serving |
| `sonata: backup (ucha1 14%)` | A Go account is capped; the named one serves, at that percent of its 5-hour window |
| `sonata: degraded` | Something is capped or blocked but traffic still flows |
| `sonata: down` | Every Go account is capped and nothing else is reachable |

`--color` wraps it in green, yellow or red. The level comes from the same
verdict as `sonata limits` and the dashboard, so they agree. It uses no
network, and it is built to be run on every refresh: the answer is cached for
10 s, a stale answer (up to 2 minutes old) is printed while a detached child
recomputes it, and **on any failure it prints nothing and exits 0**, so a broken
config leaves the status line blank rather than showing an error.

`sonata-statusline` is a second binary installed with the package: the same
command (it also takes `--color`) without loading the whole CLI first — about 40 ms on
a cache hit against roughly 400 ms for `sonata statusline`. Prefer it in a
status line script.

To add it to an existing Claude Code status line script, call it and append its
