output; it prints one line and nothing else:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ~/.claude/statusline.sh (set as "statusLine" in ~/.claude/settings.json)
input=$(cat)                                   # Claude Code's JSON on stdin
model=$(printf '%s' "$input" | jq -r '.model.display_name')
router=$(sonata-statusline --color 2>/dev/null)
printf '%s  %s\n' "$model" "$router"
```

### Slash commands

`sonata sync` also writes four commands into `.claude/commands/` beside the
agents (the project's, or `~/.claude/commands/` for a machine-scope config):

| Command | Runs | Asks Claude to |
|---|---|---|
| `/sonata` | `sonata statusline`, `sonata limits`, `sonata status` | summarize the verdict, each account and the busiest route |
| `/sonata-why` | `sonata why last` | explain the last request in plain language |
| `/sonata-accounts` | `sonata limits` | list each account as serving or capped |
| `/sonata-limits` | `sonata limits` | summarize the 5h, week and month windows and which are near a cap |

Each file runs the CLI through `!`-bash and has no logic of its own, so the
numbers are always the CLI's. Each command's `allowed-tools` is limited to
exactly the invocations it runs. `sonata sync` creates or updates only files
that carry sonata's ownership marker; a same-named file of yours is left
alone and reported as skipped, nothing is ever deleted by `sync`, and
`sonata reset` removes only the marked ones. If `.claude/commands` is a symlink
that leaves the project, nothing is written and a warning says why.

## See also

- [Alerts](alerts.md): get a message when an account is capped.
- [OpenCode Go accounts and limits](../opencode-go-limits.md): the percentages,
  two-account setup and what the router does at a cap.
- [Configuration](configuration.md): the `[alerts]`, `[ui]`, `enabled` and `plan` keys.
===== FILE 50 docs/guide/getting-started.md =====
# Getting started

This page walks through installing sonata, running `sonata init`, and
dispatching your first subagent. For what sonata is and why you might want it,
see the [README](https://github.com/zhihaohong52/sonata#readme).

## Requirements

- **Node 22+**
- **tmux** — every harness runs inside a tmux session (`brew install tmux`,
  `apt install tmux`)
- **macOS or Linux.** Windows is not supported; WSL should work but is
  untested.
- **A provider** — an API key for one of ~30 well-known providers (no harness
  needed), your Claude Code account, or at least one authenticated harness:
  [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai), [Codex CLI](https://github.com/openai/codex)
  (`codex login`), [Pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-mono) or
  [Reasonix](https://github.com/esengine/DeepSeek-Reasonix) (`reasonix setup`).
- **LiteLLM — managed, and only when a gateway needs it.** Sonata installs its
  own pinned copy (`sonata litellm install`, offered by `sonata init`); a
  gateway that speaks the Anthropic Messages API natively needs no Python at
  all. When LiteLLM *is* needed, `uv` or a `python3` in `>=3.10,<3.15` is
  required.

## Install

```bash
npm install -g @zhihaohong52/sonata
```

Later, `sonata upgrade` installs the newest release; run `sonata restart`
afterwards so the router runs it too.

## Set up a project

In the repository where you want to use it:

```bash
sonata init
```

`sonata init` detects your environment, reports anything broken with the command
that fixes it, and asks which providers, models and roles you want.

Provider setup is a menu, modeled on opencode's own `/connect`: bulk-import
everything you're already logged into elsewhere, or add providers one at a
time — including one sonata has never heard of.

```
  ███████╗ ██████╗ ███╗   ██╗ █████╗ ████████╗ █████╗
  ██╔════╝██╔═══██╗████╗  ██║██╔══██╗╚══██╔══╝██╔══██╗
  ███████╗██║   ██║██╔██╗ ██║███████║   ██║   ███████║
  ╚════██║██║   ██║██║╚██╗██║██╔══██║   ██║   ██╔══██║
  ███████║╚██████╔╝██║ ╚████║██║  ██║   ██║   ██║  ██║
  ╚══════╝ ╚═════╝ ╚═╝  ╚═══╝╚═╝  ╚═╝   ╚═╝   ╚═╝  ╚═╝

  foreign-model subagents for Claude Code

  ✓ tmux 3.7b
  ✓ opencode 1.18.19 · 520 models
  ✓ codex codex-cli 0.149.0 · 6 models

  Set up providers
  ❯ Import from other harnesses
    Add provider

  ↑↓ choose · enter confirm · ← back · esc cancel
```

**Import from other harnesses** bulk-selects providers your installed
harnesses are already authenticated for — nothing to type, nothing to
re-enter. It lists every provider with a detected credential (an OAuth grant
or a plain API key sitting in another harness's own store), whether or not
it is already configured, and pre-checks the ones that are — so the same
screen doubles as a toggle: unchecking an already-imported provider removes
it, along with its models and any role assignments that used them:

```
  Import from other harnesses

  filter: █

  ❯ ◉ codex     · expires in 8d
    ○ openai    · expires in 8d

  2 of 2 · space toggle · type to filter · enter confirm · esc cancel
```

**Add provider** searches the merged catalogue of every provider a harness
knows about plus ~30 well-known BYOK providers — or lets you type in one
sonata has never seen:

```
  Add provider

  filter: █

  ❯ acme                · opencode
    anthropic           · opencode
    codex               · codex
    deepseek            · byok
    ⋮
    Add a custom provider…

  38 of 38 · ↑↓ choose · type to filter · enter confirm · ← back · esc cancel
```

Picking a known provider offers **Run OAuth login** (for `codex` and
`github-copilot`, the two providers sonata can authenticate on its own — see
the [Native path guide](native-path.md)) or **Enter an API key**.
Picking a harness-catalogued provider then shows its models to select from:

```
  Models to enable

  filter: gpt█

  ❯ ◉ openai/gpt-5.6-sol      · GPT-5.6 Sol
    ○ openai/gpt-5.6-luna     · GPT-5.6 Luna

  2 of 13 · space toggle · type to filter · enter confirm · esc cancel
```

![Re-ranking the code-complex tier](/screenshots/tier-ranking.png)

Then it asks you to rank your selected models into `simple`, `normal` and
`complex` tiers per role — pre-sorted by a cached Artificial Analysis catalog
(`sonata catalog update`, with a free key from [artificialanalysis.ai](https://artificialanalysis.ai))
when one exists, or built-in defaults otherwise. The key is optional; without
it the wizard still works, just with coarser defaults. `complex` is ordered by
capability, and a model within 3 points of the strongest counts as tied with
it, so the cheaper one leads. `normal` leads with the knee of the
price-performance frontier, then follows capability **per task-dollar**.
`simple` is that same value order filtered to models costing at most 12 times
the best-value model per task — so it leads with the best-value model, not the
knee. Demanding work goes to the strongest model you picked, ordinary work to
the best value, and grunt work stays within the cheaper fallback chain. Set
`avoid_gateways` in
`sonata.toml` to rank a particular gateway's models last without dropping them
as fallbacks. It then asks whether the config
applies to this project or the whole machine, writes `sonata.toml`, generates
one agent per role × tier (identical tiers collapse into one agent named for
the role), offers to install the permission hook, installs the
`sonata-loop` skill, and offers to run `sonata route auto` so the generated
agents have a router to reach. Project scope writes `./sonata.toml` and
`./.claude/agents/`; machine scope writes `~/.config/sonata/sonata.toml` and
`~/.claude/agents/`, where Claude Code offers the agents in every repository.

Claude Code picks up the new agents automatically; no restart is needed. To
change a ranking later, run `sonata agents` and press enter on a tier; `r`
there resets it to the order the catalog suggests now.

Every prompt has a flag, so it also works unattended:

```bash
sonata init --yes --providers opencode/openai --models opencode-openai-gpt-5.6-sol --roles code,review --scope project
```

### BYOK (bring your own key)

Sonata does not need a harness. **Add provider** lists ~30 well-known
providers alongside anything your harnesses discovered; pick one, enter its
API key, and choose from the models it reports. A provider not on that
list — an internal proxy, a self-hosted endpoint — doesn't need to be:
**Add a custom provider…**, at the bottom of that same search list, asks for
a name, a base URL, and whether it speaks OpenAI's or Anthropic's wire
format, then drops into the same key-entry flow.

The key is stored in sonata's own key store — never in `sonata.toml`, never in
an agent file, and never on the command line. It is written only after you
confirm the summary, so cancelling the wizard stores nothing.

Unattended, with the key stored first so it stays out of argv and shell history:

```bash
sonata auth add deepseek
sonata init --yes --providers byok/deepseek --models deepseek-deepseek-v4-flash --roles code
```

BYOK models use the [native path](native-path.md), so they run
inside Claude Code's own loop, tools and permission modes.

Two things worth knowing before you pick a provider:

- **Model discovery is a convention, not a guarantee.** Sonata asks the provider
  for `GET <base_url>/models`, which every provider in its list implements. If
  yours does not answer — offline, or a different shape — the wizard asks you to
  type the model ids instead, saying which of those happened. That is a
  fallback, not an error.
- **A rejected key gets its own screen.** If the provider answers 401 or 403,
  sonata says so and offers to take a different key. It also offers to keep the
  one you gave and type ids by hand, because some providers refuse to list
  models for a key that works perfectly well for inference.
- **Claude models are ordinary models.** A tier may rank a `claude-*` id that
  a gateway serves (Copilot, OpenRouter, any other), or one on your own Claude
  Code account through a `claude` gateway with `auth = "session"` — sonata
  init offers both. Only a `claude-*` name your config does not define passes
  straight through to Anthropic. See the [Native path guide](native-path.md).

### Adding Codex models

**The wizard discovers OpenCode, Pi and Reasonix models** by provider then by
model, and **Codex through `codex app-server`'s `model/list`** (JSON-RPC over
stdio — codex has no provider dimension and takes a bare model id). A bare-id
model can also be added by hand:

```toml
[models."gpt-5-6-sol"]
harness = "codex"
id = "gpt-5.6-sol"
```

Hand-written entries survive `sonata init` — the wizard carries through any
model whose harness it does not manage.

Then run `sonata sync` to regenerate the agent files; Claude Code picks them up automatically.

## Using it

The generated agents are ordinary registry entries, so Claude selects them the
same way it selects any other subagent. Ask for one by name, or describe work
that suits it:

> "Use code-simple to convert these callbacks to async/await."

> "Use code-normal to add this flag and its tests."

> "Get review-complex to look at the auth refactor."

Choose a tier by the task, not its size: `simple` is specified closely enough
that the diff can be written without asking a question; `normal` is the default
when you know what to change but need to fit it into the surrounding code;
`complex` needs a design decision or the meaning of done is ambiguous. Size is
not difficulty: a large mechanical change is `simple`, while a three-line
interface decision is `complex`. When unsure, use `-normal`; a task that fails
review twice is re-run one tier up. The `sonata-loop` skill `sonata init` installs
(`skills/loop/SKILL.md`) drives this across a whole feature: plan, route each task
to a tier, gate behind review, and escalate `simple` to `normal` to `complex`
after repeated failures. The same folder is a Claude Code mod with a live panel:
the loop's tasks, each tier agent's current activity, the model the router
served, and an agent's diff when you select its row. `/sonata-loop panel`
toggles it once the mod is loaded — start a new session after `sonata sync`,
and `sonata doctor` checks it. See the [Native path guide](native-path.md) for
the plugin-marketplace install.

With `[auto_route]` configured (see [Configuration](configuration.md)), init
also generates a `<role>-auto` agent per role, which asks a small decision
model to pick the tier for each task. It is off unless you write that table.

They compose with everything Claude Code already does — parallel fan-out,
workflows, and `isolation: "worktree"`.
===== FILE 51 docs/guide/limitations.md =====
# Limitations

Worth knowing before you depend on this:

- **`sonata init` discovers models for four harnesses** — opencode, pi, codex
  and reasonix. Codex has no `models` subcommand, so its catalogue comes from
  `codex app-server`'s `model/list` (JSON-RPC over stdio), with a real response
  captured in `tests/fixtures/codex/model-list.json`. The `claude` harness is
  the host and is never offered for discovery.
- **Nested agents are unbounded and unattributed.** A generated agent can
  spawn further agents, and nothing counts depth — a `code-normal` agent can
  call `Agent(subagent_type: "code-normal")` on itself. Read-only roles are
  told to delegate only to other read-only roles, but that is prompt text:
  `tools:` frontmatter grants tools, not permitted argument values. `sonata
  usage` attributes spend per session rather than to the dispatch that caused
  nested cost.
- **Some dispatch runs cannot be attributed.** Two dispatches to the same
  harness in the same directory at the same time are both reported `unobservable`
  rather than split by guesswork.
- **`[budget]` counts a dispatch when it finishes.** `sonata dispatch` refuses
  to launch once a cap is reached, but one run already under way can carry
  spend past it.
- **Prompt detection is regex against TUIs sonata does not control.** Codex's
  patterns are written from captured real output in `tests/fixtures/panes/`,
  but they will still break when codex changes its interface. The `STALLED`
  timeout is the backstop. OpenCode and Pi cannot prompt at all, so there is
  nothing to detect. An answered prompt also stays in the pane, so it can be
  re-reported `PAUSED` — wasted `approve`/`wait` round trips, and a digit that
  lands in the harness's composer as text.
- **Codex through a proxy needs that proxy up.** If `~/.codex/config.toml` sets
  `openai_base_url`, `sonata doctor` checks the endpoint is listening — a dead
  proxy otherwise wastes minutes in retries before failing.
- **`opencode run --format json` is broken upstream** (v1.18.15 produces no
  output and never exits), so progress comes from pane text rather than a
  structured event stream. Pi's `--mode json` does work; the adapter keeps a
  seam for adopting it.
- **opencode's `event` table grows without bound** — 6.5 GB across 140k rows on
  the development machine, which is what produced `database is locked` under
  three concurrent dispatches. Sonata cannot prune another harness's store.
- **No streaming granularity guarantees.** Progress is whatever the harness
  prints.
- **ChatGPT's Codex endpoint occasionally returns an empty completion under
  concurrent load** instead of a 429, which LiteLLM surfaces as a 500. The
  router recognizes this specific case and re-emits it as 529 (overloaded) so
  Claude Code retries automatically instead of treating it as a hard failure.
- **Tier fallback retries only before a response starts.** The router tries
  each ranked candidate in order and returns the first one that answers with
  status < 500; once a response starts streaming there is no mid-stream
  failover to the next candidate. A candidate that fails cools down for 60
  seconds so a repeated request doesn't retry a model that just failed.
- **A conversation prefers the candidate that served its first turn.** Switching
  models mid-conversation can hand one model's thinking blocks to another,
  which the API rejects — a multi-turn agent then dies mid-task on a 400.
  Affinity and thinking-block stripping make that survivable, not impossible.

- **`normal` is optional.** A config may keep only `simple` and `complex`, preserving its previous behaviour; adding `normal` provides the uncapped value-ranked choice. `simple` is the value order capped at 12 times the best-value model's cost per task, so it leads with the best-value model while `normal` leads with the knee of the price-performance frontier.
- **A plan's overflow is invisible.** A subscription gateway's work is
  reported as covered and left out of `[budget]`. Some plans bill usage past
  their allowance per token (OpenCode Go with "Use balance" on, Chutes,
  NanoGPT, Ollama Cloud's extra credits), and nothing in a response says
  which requests did — so that spend is reported covered too.
- **`auth = "session"` needs a live Claude Code session.** Outside that context
  the session credential may be unavailable, and subscription spend is
  estimated at Anthropic list prices — a report, not a bill.
===== FILE 52 docs/guide/native-path.md =====
# Native path

The harness path runs the foreign model's *own* loop in OpenCode, Codex,
Pi, or Reasonix. The native path instead runs foreign models inside Claude
Code's own loop, tools, and permission modes, through a local routing proxy.

**The usual setup is `sonata route auto` once per project** (`sonata init`
offers it), then launching plain `claude` exactly as before. Each session
routes itself at start, the router comes up on its own, and Remote Control
keeps working. `sonata code` is for a one-off routed session somewhere you
have not set routing up.

- `sonata serve` — runs the router, and a managed LiteLLM child when any
  configured model needs one. Anthropic-native gateways go straight through
  the router and start none. The child comes up with `serve` when the config
  already needs it, and otherwise lazily, on the first request that does.
- `sonata route auto` — routes every plain `claude` session in the project
  *and* keeps Remote Control. Instead
  of leaving the routing env in the file, a SessionStart hook writes it just
  after the session launches and a SessionEnd hook removes it again, so each
  session launches from a clean file. Claude Code decides Remote Control once,
  at launch, from `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`; it re-reads the settings `env` on every
  request. Auto mode lives in that gap. Concurrent sessions are counted, so one
  ending never cuts another's routing. `sonata route manual` removes the pair.
  A session that dies without running its SessionEnd hook leaves routing on —
  the next launch loses Remote Control once; `sonata route off` resets it.
- `sonata route on` — routes every plain `claude` session by leaving
  `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` in `.claude/settings.local.json`, with a SessionStart
  hook that keeps the router up, so editor integrations, `.mcp.json` entries
  and shell aliases all go through the proxy too. Every routed session loses
  Remote Control until `sonata route off`; `sonata route status` reports which
  mode is on. Prefer `auto` unless something launches sessions in a way its
  hooks cannot reach.
- `sonata code` — launches a single routed Claude Code session
  (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` points at the local router), starting the router in
  the background if it is down. No settings are written; that session loses
  Remote Control.
- `sonata auth` — manages per-gateway keys that the router forwards to LiteLLM;
  keys live in the store and are never logged or put in a conversation.
  A stored key is only ever sent to a host bound to its gateway name — the
  provider's own endpoint, a host you confirmed with
  `sonata auth trust <gateway> <host>`, or the machine config's own URL for
  that name — so a project config pointing the name elsewhere gets no key and
  a named 502 naming the config that set the URL and the trust command,
  instead of your credential. `sonata auth add` binds nothing from a config;
  init binds the URLs typed in its own run
- `sonata auth login <gateway>` — starts LiteLLM's device login for an OAuth gateway.
  The login runs into a fresh directory that replaces the old one only on
  success, so a failed login never damages the working credential

The `claude` harness adapter completes the picture: it dispatches a
foreign-on-Claude-loop session through `sonata dispatch`, running headless
`claude -p` with no TUI. Native dispatches assume `sonata serve` is already up.

Two consequences worth knowing. First, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` is process-wide and
`isFirstPartyAnthropicBaseUrl` gates Remote Control, so a session *launched*
routed — by `sonata code`, or under `sonata route on` — loses Remote Control.
`route auto` avoids that by routing only after launch.

Second, behind a gateway Claude Code cannot verify that a model really has the
1M window it claims natively, so it budgets those models — Sonnet 5, the Fable
models, Opus 4.7+ — at 200K instead. The window silently shrinks by 80%; the
only clue is a number in `/context`. An id carrying an explicit `[1m]` is
immune, because there is nothing left to verify: `"model": "opus[1m]"` keeps
its full window where a bare `opus` does not. `sonata doctor` prints the fix
when it applies.

### Your own Claude Code account

A tier can rank Claude models served by your own Claude Code account:

    [native.gateways."claude"]
    provider = "anthropic"
    auth = "session"

    [models."opus"]
    gateway = "claude"
    id = "claude-opus-4-1"

The router forwards the session's own credential, and only to
`api.anthropic.com` — any other `base_url` is refused. Usage is priced at
Anthropic's list rates; work your Claude subscription paid for is shown as
`$x sub` and never counts toward `[budget]`. A key named exactly like a model
your main session uses (`claude-opus-4-1`) also catches that session's own
turns when it is routed.

**OpenCode Zen and Go.** The two are separate endpoints on one opencode.ai
account: Zen (pay as you go) is `https://opencode.ai/zen/v1`, Go (the
subscription) is `https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1` (models.dev now lists both
under `/inference`, and both paths answer). Both route a conversation by
an `x-opencode-session` header and refuse a request without one (400
`MissingSessionID`). Since 0.13.1 the router sends it — a stable id per
conversation — and LiteLLM forwards it only to models on an `opencode.ai`
gateway; no other client `x-*` header reaches them. Earlier versions sent none,
so no native request to an opencode.ai gateway could succeed.

## Subscription plans

Several vendors sell a flat-rate coding or token plan beside a metered API,
reached with an ordinary API key. Sonata reports a plan's work as **covered**:
valued at list price in `sonata usage` (shown as `$x sub`), never billed per
token, and left out of `[budget]`. Usage beyond a plan's allowance that the
vendor bills per token is not something a response says, so sonata cannot
see it — keep `[budget]` for metered gateways in mind if your plan overflows
to a balance.

A plan with an endpoint of its own is recognised from the gateway's
`base_url`, with nothing to configure:

| Plan | Endpoint |
|---|---|
| OpenCode Go | `opencode.ai/zen/go`, `opencode.ai/inference/go` |
| Z.ai / Zhipu GLM Coding Plan | `api.z.ai/api/coding`, `open.bigmodel.cn/api/coding` |
| Kimi For Coding | `api.kimi.com/coding`, `api.kimi.ai/coding` |
| Alibaba Coding Plan | `coding-intl.dashscope.aliyuncs.com`, `coding.dashscope.aliyuncs.com` |
| Alibaba Token Plan | `token-plan.<region>.maas.aliyuncs.com` |
| Volcengine Ark Coding / Agent Plan | `ark.cn-beijing.volces.com/api/coding`, `/api/plan` |
| Tencent Coding / Token Plan | `api.lkeap.cloud.tencent.com/coding`, `/plan` |
| Xiaomi Token Plan | `token-plan-<region>.xiaomimimo.com` |
| StepFun Step Plan | `api.stepfun.ai/step_plan`, `api.stepfun.com/step_plan` |
| KUAE Cloud Coding Plan | `coding-plan-endpoint.kuaecloud.net` |

The same vendors' pay-as-you-go endpoints (`api.z.ai/api/paas`,
`api.moonshot.ai`, `opencode.ai/zen/v1`, …) stay metered. The list follows
models.dev's provider catalogue, which opencode also reads.

Some plans share their pay-as-you-go endpoint, and only the key says which you
have: **MiniMax Token Plan, Synthetic, Chutes, NanoGPT, Ollama Cloud, Cerebras
Code, Umans AI.** Sonata treats those as metered, and `sonata doctor` names
them. If yours is a plan key, say so on the gateway:

```toml
[native.gateways."minimax"]
base_url = "https://api.minimax.io/anthropic"
provider = "anthropic"
billing = "subscription"
```

`billing = "metered"` does the opposite, for an endpoint sonata gets wrong.
`sonata doctor` lists every gateway it counts as a subscription and why.

ChatGPT (`codex-oauth`), GitHub Copilot (`copilot-oauth`) and your Claude
account (`auth = "session"`) are subscriptions through their own logins. A
SuperGrok subscription includes no API access, so xAI is always metered.

Check a plan's terms before routing it through sonata. Some limit the plan to
the vendor's listed tools — Z.ai's Coding Plan terms, for one, exclude
"SDK-based access or other third-party integrations".

See also: [Codex subscription auth](codex-subscription.md), for how the
`codex-oauth` gateway type authenticates against a ChatGPT subscription rather
than a metered API key.

## The loop panel

The `sonata-loop` skill folder `sonata init` installs is also a Claude Code mod,
which Claude Code loads from the skills folder by itself. While a loop runs it
shows a side panel (toggle it with `/sonata-loop panel`; any other
arguments start a loop as before):

- **Tasks** from the loop's plan, one line each, with a state stroke: `━━`
  active, `── done`, `· · queued`, and `─ ─` for a condition (`failed 1x`,
  an escalation). The orchestrator reports these through the panel's
  `sonata_loop` tool; nothing is inferred.
- **Agents** under their task, one line each: role and tier, the model the
  router served, tokens, elapsed time and state. A running agent adds one line
  with its current tool, step count and how long ago its last step was; one
  silent for 90 s reads `─ ─ stalled`.
- **Model and cost** come from the router. `≈` means two agents on one alias
  ran at once and the router cannot say whose request was whose, so neither is
  given a cost. A dash or `cost unknown` means unpriced or unattributable,
  never `$0`.
- **Tokens** come from Claude Code itself, so they show even when the router
  cannot be read.
- **Detail**: select a row (click, or focus the pane with `ctrl+x tab` and
  press enter) to open, beneath it, its token breakdown (input, output, cache
  read, cache write) and the edits it applied. A task's detail covers its whole
  agent tree. Only applied `Edit` and `Write` calls are diffed; when `Bash` ran
  too, the detail says so.

The panel reads the router at `http://127.0.0.1:4100` by default. With a
different `[native.ports] router`, set the mod's `router_url` option. When the
router is not reachable the footer says so and the panel keeps showing what it
last reported, with its age.

The panel can also be installed as a plugin from this repo's marketplace:

```
claude plugin marketplace add zhihaohong52/sonata
claude plugin install sonata-loop@sonata
```

Claude Code loads one plugin per name, and the installed plugin wins over any
skills-folder copy, so once it is present `sonata init` and `sonata sync` write
only the skill text and remove the panel files from their copies. Update it
with `claude plugin update sonata-loop@sonata`; `sonata doctor` says when its
version is behind the package's.
===== FILE 53 docs/guide/permission-modes.md =====
# Permission modes

Sonata mirrors your Claude Code permission mode onto the harness. A sonata
agent is never more permissive than the session that spawned it — where a
harness cannot honour a mode, sonata refuses the run rather than downgrading it
quietly.

**OpenCode:**

| Claude Code mode | agent | auto-approve |
|---|---|---|
| `plan` | `plan` (read-only) | no |
| `default` | refused for write-capable roles — see below | — |
| `acceptEdits` | `build` | yes |
| `bypassPermissions` | `build` | yes |

`opencode run` has no approval UI at all. Probed against opencode 1.18: with
permissions unset it runs commands unasked, and with `permission = { bash =
"ask" }` it does not ask either — it auto-rejects:

```
! permission requested: bash (rm file.txt); auto-rejecting
```

So `default` — "ask me first" — cannot be honoured. Rather than run an opencode
agent ungated while claiming otherwise, sonata refuses to launch a
write-capable role in `default` mode and says so. Read-only roles still run,
having nothing to ask about. To use opencode for edits, dispatch in
`acceptEdits` or `bypassPermissions`, or use a codex model, whose TUI does
prompt.

**Pi**'s tool allowlist is real enforcement, and its limits are the least
negotiable of the harnesses sonata drives. Its docs say it "intentionally does
not include built-in MCP, sub-agents, permission popups, plan mode, to-dos, or
background bash", and it has no sandbox — so like opencode it cannot honour
`default`, and refuses:

| Claude Code mode | tools |
|---|---|
| `plan` | `--tools read,grep,find,ls` |
| `default` | refused for write-capable roles |
| `acceptEdits` | all built-in tools |
| `bypassPermissions` | all built-in tools |

Unlike opencode's agent selection, pi's `--tools` allowlist is real: asked to
create a file with the write tool withheld, the model reports having no write
tool and no file appears. Note the consequence — a read-only pi run cannot
write `report.md` either, so sonata takes its terminal output as the report and
does **not** mark it degraded. A read-only run that crashes or times out is
still flagged.

Pi has no sandbox, so it draws no distinction between `acceptEdits` and
`bypassPermissions`. If you need isolation, run it in a container.

**Codex** maps onto its sandbox policy directly, and can be approved:

| Claude Code mode | invocation | sandbox |
|---|---|---|
| `plan` | `codex exec` | `read-only` |
| `default` | interactive TUI, `approval_policy=on-request` | `workspace-write` |
| `acceptEdits` | `codex exec` | `workspace-write` |
| `bypassPermissions` | `codex exec` | `danger-full-access` |

`codex exec` cannot raise an approval prompt, so `default` mode uses the
interactive TUI — otherwise a sonata agent could write without ever asking,
which would be more permissive than the session that spawned it. Sonata never
passes `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`. Its stdout stays attached
to tmux: piping it through `tee` makes codex print `Error: stdout is not a
terminal` and exit 0. After `report.md` lands, sonata clears the TUI composer
and sends Ctrl-D so the run writes its exit sentinel rather than stalling.

On first entry to a directory, the codex TUI blocks on a directory-trust
question before any work starts. Sonata surfaces it as a `PAUSED` prompt, and
`sonata doctor` warns when the project has not been trusted yet, so a
`default`-mode run does not stall on it unexpectedly.

Codex also writes its final message to a file (`-o`), so sonata has a
harness-guaranteed report and degrades to pane text far less often.

**Reasonix** has real approval cards, so like codex it can honour `default`:

| Claude Code mode | invocation | asks |
|---|---|---|
| `plan` | `reasonix run --permission-mode dontAsk` | no — denies instead |
| `default` | interactive TUI, `--permission-mode ask` | yes |
| `acceptEdits` | `reasonix run --permission-mode acceptEdits` | no |
| `bypassPermissions` | `reasonix run --permission-mode bypassPermissions` | no |

Reasonix has a `plan` mode of its own, but `reasonix run` refuses it outright —
"--permission-mode plan requires an interactive session", exit 2 — so read-only
work uses `dontAsk`, which denies without prompting. That enforcement is real
and covers the shell too: asked to read one file and write another, the model
read it fine and was refused both the write tool and a `printf … > file`
fallback. As with pi, a read-only run therefore cannot write `report.md`, so
sonata takes its terminal output as the report and does **not** mark it
degraded.

Sonata never passes `-y`/`--auto`. That flag aliases reasonix's *own* `auto`
mode, which is wider than Claude Code's — it skips risk prompts for operations
like `git push`. Since Claude's `auto` maps to `acceptEdits`, reaching for the
similarly named flag would silently widen permissions.

Two quirks worth knowing. Reasonix loads the working directory's `.mcp.json` on
top of its own config, so a dispatched model inherits whatever MCP servers your
project defines — including sonata itself, if you have it configured there;
`sonata doctor` warns when it sees one. And on a machine that has never
answered it, the very first `reasonix` invocation blocks on a telemetry consent
question before the agent starts at all, which looks exactly like a model that
never said anything — `sonata doctor` reports that as a blocker, and
`reasonix config telemetry off` clears it.

**Claude Code** (`claude -p` is headless — there is no TUI to prompt in) passes
the session's mode through, except that a read-only role — and any role
dispatched while the session is in `plan` mode — runs as `plan` and is
stripped down:

| Claude Code mode | invocation | tools |
|---|---|---|
| `plan` | `claude -p --permission-mode plan` | `--tools=Read,Grep,Glob` |
| `default` | `claude -p --permission-mode default` | full built-in set |
| `acceptEdits` | `claude -p --permission-mode acceptEdits` | full built-in set |
| `bypassPermissions` | `claude -p --permission-mode bypassPermissions` | full built-in set |

A read-only role runs as `plan` whatever mode the session is in, and so
does a write role dispatched in `plan` mode (which is also what `dontAsk`
maps to); each gets
`--tools=Read,Grep,Glob` (with `--allowedTools` of the same set) plus
`--strict-mcp-config` and no `--mcp-config`, which loads no MCP servers at all.
`--tools` restricts only the built-in set: probed live on Claude Code 2.1.284,
it left every user, project, plugin and claude.ai MCP tool reachable until
strict mode closed that. Where an enterprise `managed-mcp.json` is deployed,
`--strict-mcp-config` reads as asking to replace the managed set and Claude
Code exits at startup, so sonata falls back to `--disallowedTools=mcp__*`
there — the managed servers still start, but their tools are refused. A
read-only run cannot write `report.md`, so as with pi and reasonix its final
message is taken as the report and the run is not marked degraded.

## The permission hook

The mode is not exposed as an environment variable, so this needs a
`PreToolUse` hook — which `sonata init` offers to install, at project or global
scope. Without it, sonata assumes `default`. For codex that is simply the
cautious choice; for opencode and pi it means dispatches refuse, so
`sonata doctor` reports a missing hook as a blocker rather than letting it
surface on first use.

**`auto` mode.** Claude Code's current default mode is `auto`: it runs tool
calls its classifier judges lower-risk without prompting, and blocks the rest.
Sonata maps it to `acceptEdits`, which is the closest thing it can actually
enforce on another harness — work proceeds without prompting, as it does in the
parent session. The residual gap is worth stating plainly: the foreign harness
has no such classifier, so it will run things auto mode would have blocked.
Dispatch in `plan` mode, or to a read-only role, when that matters.

The hook writes nothing in a directory that has neither its own `sonata.toml`
(or `.sonata/`) nor a machine config. With a project `sonata.toml` or
`.sonata/`, the mode is written to `<cwd>/.sonata/session-<id>.json`; a project
relying on the machine config gets `~/.config/sonata/session-<id>.json` beside
it. So a global install does not scatter `.sonata/` directories across
unrelated repositories.
===== FILE 54 docs/guide/security.md =====
# Security

Sonata launches other coding agents on your machine. They run **as you**, with
your files and your credentials.

- **Read the [permission tables](permission-modes.md) before dispatching write-capable roles.**
  Codex and reasonix offer a real sandbox (reasonix reports its own
  `write_roots`, which follow `--dir`). Pi has none, and opencode's is
  advisory.
- **Sonata never bypasses a harness's own safety flags.** It does not pass
  `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` to codex.
- **Harness credentials stay with the harness.** Sonata reads harness config to
  report health; it does not copy, forward or log API keys. Keys live wherever
  the harness put them — opencode keeps them in `auth.json` and the
  `credential` table of `opencode.db`, for example. Sonata's own gateway keys
  (`sonata auth add`, written by `sonata init`) are separate: they live in
  sonata's key store and flow store → environment → LiteLLM on the native
  path, and never into `sonata.toml`, agent files or argv.
- **An `auth = "session"` gateway forwards your Claude Code session
  credential.** It is passed unmodified, and only ever to `api.anthropic.com` —
  a key is only ever sent to the host it belongs to.
- **A stored key is only ever sent to a host bound to its gateway name.**
  Keys are looked up by gateway name, but the `base_url` they would be sent
  to comes from a config — including a cloned repo's project config pointing
  the name at an attacker's host. A host is bound when it is the provider's
  own endpoint, you confirmed it with `sonata auth trust <gateway> <host>`,
  or it is the machine config's own URL for that name. `sonata init` binds
  the URLs you typed in its own run; `sonata auth add` binds nothing, because
  the URL it reads comes from a config a repo can carry. Anything else gets no
  key: `sonata serve` withholds it from that tenant and answers a named 502
  that names the config setting the URL and the exact trust command, and
  `sonata doctor` fails the gateway the same way, for every project it routes.
  If you did not choose a URL, remove it from that config rather than trusting
  it. Bindings live in a 0600 file beside the key store; hostnames (with a
  non-default port) compare exactly, never suffix-matched, and https only,
  except a loopback http host (`localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`). The machine
  config's own loopback URL is trusted by definition; in a project config a
  loopback URL needs an explicit `sonata auth trust`. Non-loopback plain http is
  never bindable.
  The first run after an upgrade binds, once, the hosts of the configs already
  in use that have a key; `sonata auth untrust <gateway> <host>` removes any of
  them, and `sonata auth trust-list` shows them.
- **Auto-routing sends a limited task excerpt to whatever `base_url` names.** When `[auto_route]` is set, the first message of each `-auto` subagent task is sent to that URL — TypeSafe at `api.typesafe.ai` by default, OpenRouter at `openrouter.ai/api`, or a `jev-compatible-server` you run yourself — after `<system-reminder>` blocks are removed and the text is capped at 8,000 characters. Nothing else is sent: no system prompt, tool results or later turns. The key follows the host, and a key is only ever sent to the host it belongs to: the `openrouter` key goes to `openrouter.ai` and nowhere else. A custom host gets a stored decision key only once you trust it (`sonata auth trust auto-route <host>`, or give the URL in `sonata init`). With a stored key, an untrusted host gets neither the key nor the task text: the decision is skipped and the tier falls back. With no stored key, a local decision server is sent the task text as any keyless gateway would be, so only point `base_url` at a server you run. The feature is off unless `[auto_route]` is written.

- **Prompt injection is a real risk.** A foreign model reading a hostile
  repository can be steered, and it has no classifier between it and your
  files. For untrusted code, dispatch read-only roles or run in a container.

Please report security issues privately, following
[SECURITY.md](https://github.com/zhihaohong52/sonata/blob/main/SECURITY.md),
rather than in a public issue.
===== FILE 55 docs/guide/troubleshooting.md =====
# Troubleshooting

Start with `sonata doctor` — it checks tmux, each configured harness's version
and auth, the permission hook, and the config itself: legacy layouts, tier
routing (and which of five states leaves a session unrouted), model rankings,
catalog coverage and freshness, unpriced gateways, stale MCP registrations,
auto-route decisions and the loop panel.

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| Agents don't appear in Claude Code | Run `sonata sync`; Claude Code picks up regenerated agents automatically. |
| `sonata: command not found` | The generated agents call `sonata` on your PATH. Install it with `npm install -g @zhihaohong52/sonata`, or run `npm link` in a clone if you are working on sonata itself. |
| Dispatch fails: "cannot ask for approval" | You are in `default` mode with opencode or pi, which cannot prompt. Switch to `acceptEdits`, use a codex or reasonix model, or dispatch a read-only role. |
| A tier agent errors with "all native routes … failed" | Every candidate for that tier failed. Run the `sonata dispatch --tier <role>-<tier>` command the error names, in Bash. |
| Every opencode/pi dispatch refuses | The permission hook is not installed, so sonata assumes `default`. Run `sonata init` and choose a hook scope. |
| A codex run sits in `PAUSED` at startup | Codex has not been trusted in this directory. Run `codex` there once and answer "Yes, continue". |
| A run reports `degraded` | The harness exited without writing a report. If it wrote its own fallback file (codex's `-o` message, claude's `last-message.txt`), that text is what you get; otherwise it is scraped pane output. Treat either as untrustworthy. |
| A run never finishes | It is capped by `run_timeout_seconds`. Attach with `tmux attach -t sonata-<id>` to watch it. |
| `sonata doctor` says "config predates [tiers]" | Run `sonata init` — it migrates the config to `[models]`+`[tiers]`, carrying through every previously selected model. |
| `sonata doctor` says "tier agents need a routed session" | No session routes native traffic to the router. Doctor names which of five states you are in — follow the fix it gives (usually `sonata route auto`, or `--global`). |
| A tier always picks the wrong model first | The tier is a *ranked* list and the order is the fallback order. Run `sonata agents` and re-rank it — no need to walk the whole `sonata init` wizard. |
| A tier agent's window is smaller than the model's | The alias only claims 1M when **every** native candidate in that tier — every one with a gateway — has a 1M window, since any of them may answer. Harness-lane candidates never serve the alias, so they are skipped. `sonata agents` shows each candidate's window and whether the alias carries `[1m]`. |
| A tier agent fails with `model_not_found` | The session is not routed — Claude Code sent the `sonata-*` alias to Anthropic. That is a setup problem, not a broken agent: run `sonata doctor`, then run `sonata route auto` and start a new `claude` session (or use `sonata code` for a one-off routed session). |
| Setup is in a bad state and you want to start clean | `sonata reset` (add `--global` for the machine scope) removes the config, generated agents, loop skill, CLAUDE.md block and routing hooks, while keeping your keys and usage ledger. Then run `sonata init` again. |
| Two installs disagree about a fixed bug | `sonata` on PATH runs `dist/`, not `src/`. `sonata --version` prints the version *and* the directory it ran from, which is how you tell which one answered. |
| A tier agent dies with 400 `Request is missing x-opencode-session` | sonata before 0.13.1 never sent opencode.ai its session header. Upgrade, then `sonata restart` — the running router keeps the old code until restarted. |
| An `opencode` and an `opencode-go` gateway serve the same models | Both point at the Go URL. Zen is `https://opencode.ai/zen/v1`; Go is `https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1`. Fix the `base_url` in `sonata.toml`. |
| `sonata serve --daemon` times out with "the daemon did not answer" | Something already holds the router port — often a stale daemon or another native router. Run `sonata restart` instead; it replaces the recorded occupant (the old router drains its in-flight requests first). |
